intro.heading: Primary tuition is a budget decision before it is a teaching decision
paragraphs: The IB Primary Years Programme has no external examinations. There is no paper to sit, no grade boundary to clear, no results day. That single fact changes what PYP tuition in Dubai is for, and it changes how a family should price it. In the Diploma years a parent can at least point at a mark and ask whether it has moved. In the PYP there is no mark, so a family buying tuition is buying a change in a behaviour, a skill or a piece of written work, and the only honest way to budget for that is to name the change first and the number of hours second.

Dubai makes this harder than it needs to be, because the market is opaque at the primary end. Of the providers read for this page in October 2026, three publish no price at all. Two quote in US dollars, a currency no UAE family transacts in. One publishes an hourly figure in its page copy that contradicts the price range in its own structured data. None of them separate a primary rate from a Diploma rate, even though a forty-minute reading session with an eight-year-old and a ninety-minute Higher Level chemistry session are not the same product and should not carry the same number.

So this page does the arithmetic in the open. Published market rates for a one-to-one hour in Dubai run from roughly AED 33 at the university-student end of the online market to roughly AED 650 at the named-examiner end, and the primary band sits low in that spread rather than high. A tutor travelling to a Dubai address adds the journey to the hour, and in this city the journey is rarely short. Every figure below is attributed to the provider that published it and the month it was read, because an unsourced number helps nobody and a number presented as our price when it is somebody else's is worse than no number.

The second thing a budget needs is a sense of how long primary gaps take to close. Reading fluency at seven responds to short, frequent practice and resists long sessions. Number facts behave the same way. Written expression at ten moves more slowly and needs a human reading the writing, not a worksheet. A family that buys two forty-minute sessions a week for ten weeks is usually buying something more useful than a family that buys one ninety-minute session a month for a year, and the two plans can cost almost the same.

The third thing is honesty about what tuition is not for. A child who is quiet in class because the class is taught in a language they are still acquiring needs language support, not maths support. A child whose reading has not moved in two years may need a specialist assessment rather than a tutor, and a good tutor will say so in the first fortnight rather than bill for a year. Dubai has a large and competent special educational needs sector, and pointing a family towards it costs us a client and saves them money.

What follows is a price table, the six things that move a primary quote in this emirate, the PYP framework year by year with what each phase actually reports, the Exhibition and the line a tutor will not cross, how to read a PYP report that carries no grades, the Arabic and Islamic Education requirements KHDA places on every Dubai private school, and the two exits from the PYP. IB Gram does not make home visits in Dubai; home visits are a service we run only in India. Every lesson described here happens one-to-one over live video.

dubai/ib-pyp-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Three IB programmes run in Dubai schools and a child may pass through all of them without changing campus. The PYP is the first and the longest, and the one most parents know least about, because it is the only one that ends without an examination.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.ageRange: Ages 3-12 · FS1 to Year 6 or Grade 5
programmes.description: An inquiry framework rather than a syllabus. Learning is organised around six transdisciplinary themes, and the school writes its own units of inquiry inside them. Mathematics and language are taught both within those units and as standalone strands. There is no external assessment, so a school's own reporting is the only published record of a child's progress until they leave the programme.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the PYP runs inside a private school licensed by KHDA, which means the IB framework sits on top of a federal requirement rather than replacing it. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social and Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools whatever curriculum the school is licensed for, and KHDA set a deadline of the start of the 2025-26 academic year for its current requirements. A PYP child in Dubai therefore carries two timetables at once.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against published criteria, each marked out of eight and reported as a level from one to seven. The shift from the PYP is the arrival of criterion marking: a child who has never seen a rubric suddenly has four of them per subject. Written work is assessed against descriptors rather than ticked, and the vocabulary of the descriptors has to be learned.
programmes.countryNote: Several Dubai schools run the full IB continuum on one site, so the move from Year 6 to Year 7 is a corridor rather than a transfer. That hides the size of the academic jump. Families who move instead to a British-curriculum school in Dubai meet a different problem: a Year 7 scheme of work that assumes two years of subject-separated teaching the PYP deliberately did not provide.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and creativity, activity and service. Externally examined, with internal components marked by the school and moderated by the IB. This is where the published rates in the Dubai tutoring market rise steeply, and where almost all the competitor copy in this market is aimed.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai's 2026-27 intake adds seven new private schools, four UK curriculum and three International Baccalaureate, creating 16,846 new places. More IB places at the top end eventually means more PYP places at the bottom, and the primary tutoring market in this emirate is growing from a very thin base of published information.

dubai/ib-pyp-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Primary tuition in Dubai is bought for a short list of specific gaps. These are the ones families actually ask for, in the words they use when they call. None of them is a syllabus; each is a skill a tutor can name, test and watch move.

subjects.name: Early reading and phonics
subjects.description: Decoding, blending and the irregular high-frequency words that phonics does not cover. Short sessions beat long ones at this age. Progress is measured by running a child through unseen text and counting the stumbles, not by a worksheet score.

subjects.name: Reading comprehension and inference
subjects.description: The common Dubai pattern is a child who reads aloud fluently and cannot answer a question about what they read. The gap is between decoding and meaning, and it shows up first in retrieval questions, then in inference, then in anything asking why a writer made a choice.

subjects.name: Written expression and spelling
subjects.description: Sentence variety, paragraphing, and the move from recounting an event to constructing an argument. This is the slowest of the primary gaps to close and the one that most needs a person reading the actual writing each week rather than marking a tick-box exercise.

subjects.name: Number sense and mental calculation
subjects.description: Number bonds, place value and the facts that have to be automatic before anything else works. A child counting on their fingers in Year 4 is not slow at maths; they are carrying a load in working memory that should have been retired, and that is fixable in weeks with frequent short practice.

subjects.name: Fractions, decimals and percentages
subjects.description: The single largest source of primary maths distress in Dubai classrooms. Most of the trouble is conceptual rather than procedural: a child who cannot picture three quarters cannot be taught to add it to a half by rule, and the rule will fail the moment the question is phrased differently.

subjects.name: Measurement, data and early geometry
subjects.description: Units and conversion, perimeter against area, reading a scale that does not start at zero, and interpreting a graph rather than reciting it. These topics are heavily represented in PYP unit assessments because they sit naturally inside inquiry work, and they are often the first place a reporting gap appears.

subjects.name: Mathematical word problems and reasoning
subjects.description: Turning a sentence into a calculation. Children who can perform every operation in isolation often freeze here, and the block is usually linguistic rather than mathematical, which matters in a city where a large share of primary pupils are learning in their second or third language.

subjects.name: Science inquiry and recording
subjects.description: Writing a method someone else could follow, recording results in a table that makes sense, and separating what was observed from what was concluded. These are the habits the MYP will assess formally from Year 7, and a PYP child who builds them early arrives with an advantage.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Mandatory in Dubai private schools for non-Arab pupils, taught in the language of the school's licensed curriculum for the moral and social strands. Most families who ask for help here want script fluency and vocabulary retention, which respond to short, daily, low-stakes practice.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first language and Islamic Education
subjects.description: Separate provision from the additional-language stream, taught with Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction. KHDA requires schools to run separate classes for Arab and non-Arab pupils in these subjects, and tuition should mirror whichever stream the child is placed in rather than blending the two.

dubai/ib-pyp-home-tutor.regionsIntro: Where a family lives in Dubai changes the practical shape of a primary lesson more than it changes the price. The variables that matter are the school run, the hour the youngest child becomes useless, and whether there is a room in the home where a forty-minute lesson can happen without a sibling in it.

regions.name: Arabian Ranches and Arabian Ranches 2
regions.note: Villa communities with primary schools inside the gate, so the school run is short and a 16:00 session is realistic. The constraint here is swimming and football rather than traffic: most families end up protecting a 16:45 slot on two fixed weekdays.

regions.name: Dubai Hills Estate
regions.note: A young population with a high share of Foundation Stage and lower-primary children. Parents commonly want two short sessions a week rather than one long one, which suits early reading and number facts and costs about the same.

regions.name: Jumeirah Village Circle and Jumeirah Village Triangle
regions.note: Apartment-dense, with several primary schools serving a large catchment. The practical issue is a quiet surface to work on: a cleared dining table with the television off changes a lesson more than any software does.

regions.name: Mirdif and Al Warqa
regions.note: Established family districts feeding IB continuum and British primaries, with a high proportion of Arabic-first households. Requests here often pair a maths or English gap with Arabic first-language support in the same week.

regions.name: Al Barsha and Al Barsha South
regions.note: The densest concentration of IB World Schools in the emirate, and the easiest place in Dubai to find three PYP schools within a short drive. Families here often compare schools mid-primary, which generates transition work rather than remedial work.

regions.name: Emirates Hills, The Springs and The Meadows
regions.note: Low-density villa communities with long internal drives. This is where a visiting tutor's travel time is most expensive and where a video lesson most clearly wins: the hour starts at the hour rather than ten minutes after it.

regions.name: Dubai Silicon Oasis and Academic City
regions.note: Mixed housing beside a cluster of schools and universities. Session timing here is set by the parent's commute home rather than the child's, so later evening slots are more common than elsewhere in Dubai.

regions.name: Al Jaddaf and Sobha Hartland
regions.note: Newer riverside communities with recently opened international schools and a young intake. Many children here have changed school at least once, which puts curriculum continuity rather than attainment at the centre of the first conversation.

schoolClusters.city: Al Barsha, Emirates Hills and Umm Suqeim
schoolClusters.note: The emirate's thickest cluster of IB continuum schools, with several running the PYP, MYP and Diploma on one campus. Families from this group most often ask for lower-primary reading support and for help with the final PYP year, where the Exhibition lands.

schoolClusters.city: Mirdif, Al Jaddaf and the eastern communities
schoolClusters.note: IB and American-curriculum primaries serving a largely Arabic-first and South Asian intake. Requests from this cluster frequently combine English comprehension with Arabic first-language work, which KHDA requires schools to timetable as a separate stream from Arabic as an additional language.

schoolClusters.city: Arabian Ranches, Dubai Hills and the Springs
schoolClusters.note: British-curriculum primaries sitting alongside IB schools in the same catchment, so this is where mid-primary transfers between frameworks happen most often. The work here is usually about closing a scheme-of-work gap rather than fixing an attainment gap.

dubai/ib-pyp-home-tutor.modesIntro: Primary tuition breaks into a small number of shapes, and the right one is set by the child's age and the gap rather than by the family's budget. A seven-year-old and an eleven-year-old should not be sold the same session length.

modes.title: Two short sessions a week, forty minutes each
modes.description: The default for early reading, phonics and number facts. Frequency does the work at this age, not duration. Two forty-minute slots cost roughly the same as one eighty-minute slot and produce considerably more, because a six-year-old's useful attention runs out well before eighty minutes and because the gap between sessions is where retrieval happens.

modes.title: One weekly session of sixty minutes
modes.description: Suits Years 4 to 6, where the work is comprehension, written expression, fractions and reasoning rather than mechanics. An hour is long enough to read a piece of writing together, redraft part of it, and set something to attempt before the next session. Beyond an hour, most upper-primary children stop producing and start performing.

modes.description: The last year of the programme carries the Exhibition and, in most Dubai schools, the secondary transition process at the same time. A short block of weekly sessions through that term keeps research skills, note-taking and written structure moving without a tutor touching the work the child must own.

sections.heading: What a Dubai parent is actually buying when they search for a PYP tutor
paragraphs: An IB PYP tutor in Dubai is hired to change one named thing, because the programme gives you nothing else to aim at. There is no external examination in the Primary Years Programme and no published grade. The school's own reporting is the whole record, and most Dubai PYP reports are written in the language of the framework rather than the language of attainment. A parent reading that a child is a developing communicator has been told something real but cannot price it.

So the first conversation is a translation exercise. Four requests cover most of what families in this emirate ask for. The first is reading: a child in Year 2 or 3 whose decoding has stalled, or an older child who reads aloud well and understands little of it. The second is number: a child in Year 4 still counting on fingers, or a child in Year 5 who cannot hold a fraction in mind. The third is writing, which arrives later and moves more slowly than either. The fourth is transition, where nothing is wrong at all and the family is buying continuity across a school move.

What separates these requests is not difficulty but tempo. Reading and number facts respond to short, frequent, low-stakes practice and can move visibly inside six weeks. Written expression needs a reader, a redraft and patience, and six weeks will show a change in one paragraph rather than in a report. Transition work is finite: there is a list, you work through it, you stop. Pricing a request without first deciding which of these it is produces either a wasted year or a block of hours bought in the wrong month.

The last part of the translation is deciding whether a tutor is the right purchase at all. If a child's difficulty is in the language of instruction rather than the subject, the gap closes faster with language support. If reading has not moved across two full years despite good teaching, a specialist assessment is the next step and a weekly tutor will mask the problem rather than solve it. Dubai is well supplied with that expertise. Saying so early is part of the job.
bullets: Name the change before you count the hours
Reading and number facts move faster than written expression
Transition work is finite and should end
Language and specialist needs are different purchases

sections.heading: What PYP tutoring costs in Dubai, in dirhams
paragraphs: Published hourly rates for one-to-one tutoring in Dubai span a factor of roughly twenty, from the low thirties to the high six hundreds in dirhams. The primary end sits low in that spread. A qualified primary teacher working online in this market publishes figures in the region of AED 150 to AED 300 an hour; the budget online tier, largely university students, advertises from the thirties to the sixties; a tutor travelling to a Dubai address is quoted between roughly AED 180 and AED 500 once the journey is inside the number.

Every figure in the table below was published by the provider named and read in October 2026. They are market rates, not IB Gram prices. We do not publish a primary price list on this page, because the honest answer to what a block of sessions will cost depends on session length, frequency and whether the child needs one subject or two, and a number printed before that conversation would be a guess dressed as a quote. The free trial lesson and the consultation that follows it are where a real figure comes from.

Read the monthly packages carefully. A published online package of AED 799 for eight sessions works out near AED 100 a session, which looks cheap against the hourly bands until you check the session length and what counts as a session. An in-home monthly package advertised between AED 1,599 and AED 1,799 for four two-hour visits is a different product again: eight contact hours, four journeys, and a rate per hour that lands in the middle of the in-home band rather than at its bottom. Comparing packages on the headline number rather than on minutes of one-to-one contact is the most common way a Dubai family overpays.

One more line belongs in a primary budget and almost never appears in a quote. Short sessions are better for young children and short sessions are worse value per journey, which is precisely why visiting tutors push for ninety minutes and why a forty-minute lesson is easy to buy when nobody has to drive anywhere. The format a family chooses quietly decides the session length, and for a seven-year-old the session length decides whether the money does anything.

sections.heading: Six things that move a primary tuition quote in this emirate
paragraphs: Two Dubai families can ask for the same thing in the same week and be quoted figures that differ by a factor of four. Almost none of that spread is about quality. It is about six variables, and each one can be checked in a single question before any money moves. A provider who cannot answer them plainly is a provider whose number is not a number.

Format comes first and moves the figure furthest. A journey across Dubai at 16:30 is not a small input, and a visiting tutor either prices it in or absorbs it by stretching the lesson. Session length comes second, and at primary it works in reverse to what most parents assume: the shorter session is usually the better buy and the worse deal per journey, which is why it is hard to find in-home. Subject rarity matters less at primary than at Diploma, with one exception: Arabic as a first language and Islamic Education are a genuinely thin specialist market in this emirate.

The remaining three are timing, continuity and paperwork. A request made in the week a school report lands is quoted differently from the same request made in September. A family buying a named block of ten sessions is quoted differently from a family buying open-ended weekly support. And a provider who issues a written scope, a cancellation rule and a receipt is doing work that a provider taking cash for an hour is not; some of the difference in the rate is that work, and it is worth paying for. What is not worth paying for is a premium justified by a credential claim nobody will put in writing.

The table below sets out each variable, the direction it pushes the number, roughly how far, and the question that tests it. Use it as a script. The answers tell you more about a provider than the rate does.

sections.heading: The PYP phase by phase, and what each one actually reports
paragraphs: The Primary Years Programme runs from age three to age twelve and organises everything around six transdisciplinary themes: who we are, where we are in place and time, how we express ourselves, how the world works, how we organise ourselves, and sharing the planet. Schools write their own units of inquiry inside those themes, which is why two Dubai PYP schools can teach the same year group entirely different content and both be doing it correctly. Mathematics and language are taught inside the units and also as standalone strands.

Alongside the themes sit the components a report is most likely to quote: the key concepts that drive an inquiry, the approaches to learning grouped as thinking, research, communication, social and self-management skills, the learner profile attributes, and action. Those words are not padding. They are the categories the school is assessing in, and a parent who learns them can read a report properly instead of hunting it for a grade that is not there.

What changes across the phases is the balance between the inquiry and the standalone strands. In the early years almost everything is play-based and the reporting is narrative. By the middle of primary, mathematics and language reporting becomes recognisably subject-shaped, and this is where a gap in number facts or decoding becomes visible as a comment rather than a mark. In the final year the Exhibition arrives, and with it the first long independent piece of work most PYP children have produced.

The table maps those phases onto Dubai year names, says what the school is reporting at each stage, and says what tuition can realistically change there. Note how little of it is content coverage. At primary the thing a tutor can actually shift is a skill, and the earlier in this table you are, the faster it shifts.

sections.heading: The Exhibition, and the line a tutor will not cross
paragraphs: The Exhibition sits at the end of the Primary Years Programme and is usually the first piece of extended, self-directed work a child has produced. It is collaborative, it runs over weeks rather than days, and it ends in a presentation to an audience that includes parents. For a ten-year-old who has never had to hold a question in mind for a month, it is a genuine shock, and it is the single most common reason a Dubai family contacts a tutor about a child who has never needed one.

What a tutor can legitimately do here is narrow and useful. A question can be tested: most Exhibition difficulties are caused by a question that is too broad to answer or too narrow to sustain, and twenty minutes spent reshaping it saves three weeks. Note-taking can be taught, because most children at this age copy rather than note. Sources can be discussed, including why a search result is not automatically a source. Structure can be rehearsed on a different topic entirely. Presenting aloud can be practised until the child stops reading from a card.

What a tutor must not do is produce any part of the work. The Exhibition has to be the child's, in their words, from their notes, and a tutor who supplies sentences has taken the one thing the exercise exists to develop. This is not a style preference; it is the same academic-honesty principle that governs assessed work all the way up to the Diploma, and a child who learns at ten that an adult will supply the hard part learns a habit that becomes a malpractice problem at eighteen. We teach, we question, we give feedback on what the child has made, and we keep a record of which is which.

The practical version of that boundary is a rule about artefacts. Every session leaves something the child made and something the tutor wrote, and the two are never mixed. If a parent cannot tell from the record whose words are whose, the record is not doing its job. Families who want a clearer version of this line, written in the language the IB itself uses, should ask the school's PYP coordinator for the current academic honesty policy; every school has one and most parents have never read it.

sections.heading: Reading a PYP report when there are no grades on it
paragraphs: A Dubai PYP report is a long document that often tells a parent less than a short one would. It is written in framework language, it is organised by unit rather than by subject, and it is careful not to rank. All of that is deliberate and defensible. It is also why so many families arrive at a tutoring conversation knowing something is wrong and unable to say what. The report has to be read with a method, and the method is not complicated.

Start with the standalone strands rather than the units. Mathematics and language usually appear as their own sections, and they are the only part of the document that behaves like a subject report. Read the verbs. A child who is described as beginning to use a strategy is at a different point from one who is applying it independently, and that distance is the whole of the information you are looking for. Then read the approaches-to-learning comments, because self-management and research comments predict secondary difficulty better than attainment comments do.

Next, read for what is absent. Reports are positive by convention, so the significant signal is often a strand that is described briefly or in general terms while others are described with examples. A teacher who writes three specific sentences about a child's measurement work and one generic sentence about their writing has told you where the writing is. Finally, take the report to the parent meeting with three written questions rather than a feeling, and ask for one piece of the child's own work for each question.

Two Dubai-specific records sit alongside the report and answer different things. Your school's KHDA inspection report describes the school's provision on a six-band scale from Outstanding to Very Weak and says nothing about your child. Any externally marked benchmark test the school uses describes your child against a wider population and says nothing about the PYP. Ask the school which benchmark assessments it administers and when, because that answer varies between Dubai schools and it changes what evidence is available to you.
bullets: Read the standalone mathematics and language strands first
Read the verbs: beginning, developing, applying independently
Treat a vague strand as the signal, not the filler
Separate what describes the school from what describes your child

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies from the first year of school
paragraphs: Every Dubai private school teaches Arabic, Islamic Education and Social and Moral Studies regardless of which international curriculum it is licensed for. This is a federal requirement before it is a KHDA one: private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. KHDA's current mandatory-subject requirements had to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, and April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April.

The structural detail that catches families out is streaming. KHDA requires schools to organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and states that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, Arabic is the primary language for Social Studies for Arab pupils, and non-Arabs are taught Islamic Education and the moral, social and cultural strand in the language of the school's licensed curriculum.

Two further requirements matter to anyone buying tuition in these subjects. Schools must ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach them, which is a concrete and checkable credential rather than a marketing line. And for the mandatory subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited, so a tutor who proposes to teach from their own imported workbook in these streams is proposing something the school cannot use.

Timetabling is set in the same guidance. Mandatory-subject instructional time is calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the total weekly time is met, and it is advised that any mandatory-subject lesson runs at least twenty-five minutes. That forty-minute unit is a useful anchor for primary tuition generally: it is roughly the length a Dubai school has already decided a primary lesson should be.

sections.heading: Leaving the PYP: into the MYP, or into a British Year 7
paragraphs: There are two exits from a Dubai PYP school and they produce different problems. Staying inside the IB continuum means moving into the Middle Years Programme, usually on the same campus, which hides the size of the change. The child meets eight subject groups, each with published criteria marked out of eight and reported as a level from one to seven, and a rubric vocabulary nobody has taught them. Children who coped happily with inquiry often struggle for a term with being marked against descriptors.

Moving to a British-curriculum school in Dubai produces the opposite problem. Year 7 schemes of work assume two years of subject-separated teaching with formal written methods, and the PYP deliberately did not provide that. The gaps are predictable and short: long multiplication and division set out formally, timed arithmetic, spelling conventions taught as rules, and the expectation of a full written answer in a subject exercise book. None of this means a PYP child is behind; it means the receiving school's starting assumptions differ from the leaving school's ending ones.

A third route matters in this emirate because of how many families move mid-primary. Dubai licenses seventeen curricula and the British curriculum accounts for the largest share of private-school enrolment, with the Indian curriculum next, the American curriculum after that and the IB a smaller share of the total. A child can therefore move within Dubai and change framework entirely without changing city. That is a transition problem, not an attainment problem, and it responds to a short, finite block of work rather than open-ended tuition.

Treat any of these moves as a list, not a condition. Get the receiving school's scheme of work for the first term, get the leaving school's final report, lay them side by side, and the gap is usually six to ten sessions long. Then stop. A transition block that drifts into permanent weekly tuition is a sign nobody wrote the list down at the start.

sections.heading: A tutor crossing Dubai against forty minutes on live video
paragraphs: This page is written for a search that contains the words home tutor, and the honest answer to it has two halves. The first half is what an in-home arrangement in Dubai actually involves: a journey at the worst hour of the day, a lesson length chosen partly to justify that journey, a tutor pool limited to whoever lives within reach of your community, and a rate between roughly AED 180 and AED 500 an hour with the travel folded in somewhere. For some families that is the right purchase, and the market that sells it is large.

The second half is what IB Gram actually does. IB Gram does not make home visits in Dubai, and we do not run in-person lessons in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we provide only in India. Every lesson described on this page is one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time. We say that plainly rather than leaving a parent to discover it after an enquiry, because two providers found in this market route UAE families to numbers outside the UAE without saying so, and that is a trust failure before it is anything else.

The case for the online format at primary is not that it is cheaper, although removing the journey does remove a cost. It is that the two things that matter most for a young child, session length and tutor fit, stop being constrained by geography. A forty-minute lesson twice a week is affordable and practical when nobody is driving; it is close to impossible to buy in-home. And a family in Emirates Hills or Arabian Ranches gets a primary reading specialist rather than the best available tutor within a twenty-minute radius of their gate, which in a low-density villa community is a meaningfully smaller pool.

There are real losses and they belong on the page. A tutor on a screen cannot tidy a desk, cannot notice a sibling arriving, and cannot read a room the way an adult in it can. With children under six, a parent has to be nearby for the first few sessions. Handwriting work needs a document camera or a phone propped over the page. None of these is fatal and all of them are specific; the table sets them against what the format gains.

sections.heading: If the budget is fixed, where the dirhams do the most work
paragraphs: Most families arrive with a monthly figure in mind rather than an hourly one, and the useful question is not how many hours it buys but which hours. Primary tuition has a sharply uneven return: the same money spent on different things produces very different outcomes, and the ranking is fairly stable across children. Spending in the wrong order is the most common waste in this part of the market, and it costs more than choosing the wrong provider.

First call on a limited budget is anything automatic that has not become automatic. Letter-sound knowledge at five, blending at six, number bonds at seven, times tables at eight. These are load-bearing: a child who has not retired them is spending working memory on them in every lesson, and they respond to short frequent practice better than to anything else money can buy. A modest budget spent on two twenty-five to forty-minute sessions a week for ten weeks here will usually outperform the same money spent anywhere else in the primary curriculum.

Second call is comprehension, because it compounds and because it is the gap most often missed. A child who decodes fluently can mask a comprehension problem for years, and Dubai classrooms are full of confident readers who cannot answer an inference question. Third call is written expression, which is worth funding only if you can commit to a reader every week over a term; bought in short bursts it produces very little. Fourth is anything content-specific for a transition, which is finite and should be bought as a block with a defined end.

What a fixed budget should not buy first is an hour a week of general homework supervision, which is the easiest thing to purchase in this market and the least likely to change anything. Nor should it buy a premium tier aimed at examination candidates; the published AED 500 to AED 650 band in Dubai exists for Diploma and A Level work and no provider offers a reason to apply it to a nine-year-old. Free moves matter too: ten minutes of reading aloud daily, a timed tables app, and one honest conversation with the class teacher cost nothing and reduce the hours you need to buy.

process.title: Tell us the gap, not the year group
process.description: A first message that says reading has stalled in Year 3, or fractions collapsed in Year 5, is worth more than a message that says our daughter needs a PYP tutor. Name the behaviour you can see at home and send the most recent report and one piece of the child's own recent work.

process.title: A free trial lesson, with the parent nearby
process.description: One trial lesson per family, no card required and nothing to pay. For a primary child the trial is mostly diagnosis: unseen reading, a short calculation check, and a piece of writing attempted live. A parent sitting within earshot for this first session is a feature, not an intrusion.

process.title: A written plan with a named change in it
process.description: After the trial you receive a short plan that names the gap, the session length and frequency we recommend for that age, what we expect to see move, and roughly when. If the honest answer is that a tutor is the wrong purchase, the plan says that instead and names what to do.

process.title: Weekly sessions that leave a record
process.description: Each session ends with the child's own marked work and a one-line note to the parent saying what was practised and what to attempt before next time. Nothing in the record mixes the tutor's words with the child's, which matters from the PYP onwards.

process.title: A six-week review against the trial check
process.description: At six weeks we re-run the same unseen check used in the trial and compare. Primary gaps that respond at all usually show movement by then. If nothing has moved we change the tutor, change the plan, or tell you to stop; continuing unchanged is not one of the options.

whyPoints.title: A price conversation with real numbers in it
whyPoints.description: Published Dubai rates in dirhams, attributed to the provider and the month they were read, with the packages converted to a per-session figure. We do not print an IB Gram primary price list before a trial, because a number set before the diagnosis would be a guess.

whyPoints.title: Session lengths chosen for the child's age
whyPoints.description: Forty minutes twice a week for early reading and number facts; sixty minutes once a week for upper-primary comprehension and writing. The format makes short sessions practical, which is the main reason it suits primary at all.

whyPoints.title: The academic honesty line held from age ten
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches, questions and gives feedback on what the child has made. No part of an Exhibition or any other assessed piece is supplied by us, and the record keeps the child's words and the tutor's feedback visibly separate.

whyPoints.title: The Arabic and Islamic Education streams kept separate
whyPoints.description: Dubai schools must stream Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies by group, and may not combine them. Tuition follows whichever stream the school has placed the child in rather than blending the two into something the school cannot use.

whyPoints.title: Honest limits, written down before you pay
whyPoints.description: If a gap looks like a language-of-instruction issue or needs a specialist assessment, we say so and point you to it. If no primary specialist in the exact stream is free, we say that rather than matching whoever is available.

whyPoints.description: Lessons are one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram runs no centre, office or branch in the UAE and makes no home visits here, and we would rather say that on the page than in an email after an enquiry.

faqs.question: How much does a PYP tutor cost per hour in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Published rates for one-to-one tutoring in Dubai, read in October 2026, run from about AED 33 an hour at the budget online end to AED 650 at the named-examiner end. The primary band sits low in that range: a qualified teacher working online publishes figures around AED 150 to AED 300, and a tutor travelling to a Dubai address is quoted roughly AED 180 to AED 500 with the journey folded in. Those are other providers' figures, not ours. We do not publish a primary price list before a free trial lesson, because session length and frequency change the total more than the hourly rate does.

faqs.question: Does the IB Primary Years Programme have exams?
faqs.answer: No. The PYP has no external examinations and no published grades. Assessment is internal: the school reports against the framework's own language, usually unit by unit, with standalone mathematics and language strands alongside. The final year ends with the Exhibition, which is an extended collaborative inquiry rather than a test. This is why PYP tuition has to be bought against a named skill instead of a target grade. Many Dubai schools also administer externally marked benchmark assessments to compare pupils with a wider population; which ones, and when, varies between schools, so ask your school directly rather than assuming.

faqs.question: My child is in Year 3 and reads below age level. Is a tutor the right move?
faqs.answer: Often yes, and lower primary is the fastest-moving window in the programme. Decoding, blending and high-frequency words respond well to two short sessions a week, and six weeks is usually enough to see movement on an unseen reading check. Two cautions. If the child is learning in a language they are still acquiring, language support will do more than reading support. And if reading has not moved across two full years despite good classroom teaching, ask the school about a specialist assessment before buying weekly tuition, because a tutor can mask that pattern rather than resolve it.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the PYP Exhibition without breaking the rules?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a clear boundary. A tutor can test and reshape the research question, which is where most Exhibition trouble starts; teach note-taking rather than supplying notes; discuss what makes a source usable; rehearse structure on an unrelated topic; and practise presenting aloud until the child stops reading from a card. What a tutor must not do is supply any sentence that ends up in the child's work. The Exhibition exists to develop exactly the skills an adult would be taking over. Ask your school's PYP coordinator for its academic honesty policy; every school has one.

faqs.question: Will a PYP tutor follow my child's school units of inquiry?
faqs.answer: Partly, and less than parents expect. Dubai PYP schools write their own units inside the six transdisciplinary themes, so two schools teaching the same year group may cover entirely different content and both be correct. A tutor can and should know what the current unit is, so sessions connect to classroom work. But the thing tuition actually moves is a skill in the standalone mathematics or language strands, and those travel across units. Chasing the unit content week by week produces a tutor who revises alongside the class rather than one who closes a gap.

faqs.question: How long should a tutoring session be for a seven-year-old?
faqs.answer: Forty minutes is a sensible ceiling, and twenty-five to thirty minutes is often better for phonics or number facts. KHDA calculates mandatory-subject instructional time on a forty-minute lesson unit and advises at least twenty-five minutes for any such lesson, which is a reasonable anchor for primary tuition generally. Two short sessions a week beat one long one at this age because retrieval happens in the gap between them. The reason ninety-minute primary lessons exist in this market is that a tutor who has driven across Dubai needs the hour to be worth the journey.

faqs.question: How do Dubai schools report PYP progress if there are no grades?
faqs.answer: Through narrative comments organised by unit, with standalone mathematics and language strands, plus comments on the approaches to learning and the learner profile. Read the strands first and read the verbs: beginning to use a strategy is a different position from applying it independently, and that distance is the information you want. Then read for vagueness, because reports are positive by convention and a strand described in general terms while others carry specific examples is usually the signal. Take three written questions to the parent meeting and ask for one piece of your child's own work per question.

faqs.question: Is Arabic tutoring separate from PYP tutoring in Dubai?
faqs.answer: It is a separate stream and should stay one. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social and Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools whatever curriculum they are licensed for, and KHDA requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab pupils in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, with combined classes prohibited. Standard Arabic is the language of instruction for the first-language and Arab Islamic Education streams. Tuition should follow whichever stream the school has placed the child in. KHDA also prohibits different or additional content in these subjects without prior Ministry of Education permission.

faqs.question: How do I tell whether my child needs maths help or reading help?
faqs.answer: Test the language, not the maths. Give the child a word problem to read aloud and then ask them to say what it is asking for in their own words, before any calculation. A child who performs every operation correctly in isolation but freezes on word problems usually has a comprehension block rather than a mathematical one, which matters in a city where most primary pupils are learning in a second or third language. If the retelling is accurate and the calculation still fails, the gap is mathematical. A trial lesson should run both checks before anyone recommends a subject.

faqs.question: What changes when my child moves from the PYP into the MYP?
faqs.answer: Criterion marking arrives. The MYP has eight subject groups, each assessed against published criteria marked out of eight and reported as a level from one to seven, and the descriptors have their own vocabulary that nobody has taught your child. Work is measured against a rubric rather than commented on. Children who thrived on inquiry often have a difficult first term purely because they are answering the wrong thing well. Two to four sessions on reading a rubric and writing to it does most of the work, usually alongside some practice on independent subject writing to a set length.

faqs.question: We are moving from a PYP school to a British school in Dubai. What should we prepare?
faqs.answer: Ask the receiving school for its first-term scheme of work and lay it beside your child's final PYP report. The gaps are predictable and short: formal long multiplication and division set out in a standard written layout, timed arithmetic, spelling taught as rules, and the expectation of a full written answer in a subject exercise book. Dubai licenses seventeen curricula and the British curriculum carries the largest share of private-school enrolment, so this move is common. Treat it as a list of six to ten sessions with a defined end rather than open-ended weekly tuition.

faqs.question: Does a primary tutor in Dubai need a government permit?
faqs.answer: Yes. Private tutoring in the UAE requires a MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students, and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. MoHRE's own service is called Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, applied for through its app, website and e-services, with a stated two-working-day completion time. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published.

faqs.question: How many weeks before we can tell whether primary tutoring is working?
faqs.answer: Six weeks, if the plan names a measurable check at the start and re-runs it. For decoding, blending, number bonds and tables, movement on an unseen check inside six weeks is a reasonable expectation. Comprehension takes longer and shows up first as better answers to retrieval questions, then to inference. Written expression is the slowest and will show a change in one paragraph rather than in a report. If nothing has moved at six weeks, change the tutor, change the plan or stop. Continuing unchanged while hoping is the expensive option.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover maths, English and Arabic for a PYP child?
faqs.answer: Maths and English together, usually yes at primary level, and often sensibly so because the two gaps interact through word problems and written answers. Arabic is different. Arabic as a first language and Islamic Education are specialist streams taught with Standard Arabic as the language of instruction, KHDA requires schools to run them separately from the non-Arab provision, and the pool of primary specialists in that exact stream is genuinely thin in this market. Expect a second tutor there. If no specialist in the right stream is free, we will say so rather than matching whoever is available.

faqs.question: Why are the lessons online when I searched for a home tutor in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Because that is the phrase parents type, and we would rather answer it honestly than quietly. IB Gram does not make home visits in Dubai; home visits are a service we run only in India. Every lesson is one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time. At primary the format has a specific advantage: short sessions twice a week become practical when nobody is driving across the city at 16:30, and session length matters more than almost anything else for a child under ten. The losses are real too, and parents of children under six should plan to sit nearby.

dubai/ib-pyp-home-tutor.closingHeading: Start with a trial lesson and a number you can check
dubai/ib-pyp-home-tutor.closingBody: Send the most recent report, one piece of your child's own recent work, and a sentence describing what you can see at home. The trial lesson is free, one per family, with nothing to pay and no card required, and for a primary child it is mostly diagnosis: unseen reading, a short calculation check and a piece of writing attempted live. After it you get a written plan naming the gap, the session length and frequency we recommend for that age, and what we expect to move by week six. If the honest answer is that a tutor is the wrong purchase, the plan will say so and tell you who to call instead.

dubai/ib-pyp-maths-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach primary mathematics, which is a different craft from teaching Diploma mathematics. Each works in short focused blocks appropriate to a child aged five to twelve, on one strand at a time, with the session note telling you exactly what was practised.

intro.heading: Pricing a primary maths hour when the school report contains no numbers
paragraphs: Dubai parents asking about primary maths tutoring are working with almost no information. The PYP does not produce percentages, so the report says your child is developing an understanding of place value and leaves you to guess whether that is a problem. Published tutoring rates in this emirate span a factor of twenty, from AED 33 an hour to AED 650. And the sales conversation usually starts with a package rather than a diagnosis. It is an unusually hard spending decision for an unusually small amount of actual money.

So this page is built around the number. An IB PYP maths tutor in Dubai sits somewhere on a published rate ladder, and the useful question is not what the top of that ladder costs but what each rung actually buys for a child in Year 2 or Year 5. A university student at AED 45 an hour can supervise homework and will not identify why a nine-year-old cannot subtract across a zero. A trained primary teacher at AED 200 can, and often needs fewer hours to do it. The cost per hour and the cost per fixed problem are different numbers, and only one of them matters.

The second thing we price here is the alternatives, because a tutoring page that pretends tutoring is always the answer is not worth reading. The school's own maths intervention group costs nothing and is frequently the correct first step. A well-chosen app subscription at a few dirhams a month fixes fluency, which is the most common actual problem, better than a paid adult does. Splitting one session between siblings halves the rate and halves the usefulness. All four options appear in the tables below with honest verdicts.

The maths content matters too, because it determines how many hours anything takes. PYP mathematics is organised into five strands: number, pattern and function, measurement, shape and space, and data handling. They are not equally responsive to tutoring. Number fluency moves quickly with short daily practice and barely needs a tutor at all once the method is clear. Pattern and function, which is early algebra, moves slowly and benefits from a teacher who can see the misconception. Spending the same money on the wrong strand is the most common waste in Dubai primary tutoring, and it is entirely avoidable.

A word on context. KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there will be no increase in school fees for private schools in Dubai for the 2026-27 academic year, under Dubai's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion. For families whose tutoring budget is whatever the fee rise would have taken, that is useful news and a reasonable moment to decide deliberately rather than by default. Lessons here are one-to-one on live video across the UAE; IB Gram does not send tutors to homes in Dubai, and the comparison below explains what that costs and saves.

dubai/ib-pyp-maths-tutor.programmesIntro: What a maths hour is worth depends heavily on the child's age, because the content and the attention span both change. These are the stages we cover for Dubai families, with the spending question each one raises.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme, early years
programmes.description: Counting, one-to-one correspondence, subitising, early comparison of quantity. Almost nothing here needs a paid tutor, and the money is better spent on nothing at all. The exception is a child with an identified processing difficulty, where a specialist assessment rather than a maths tutor is the useful purchase.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai nurseries and foundation years vary widely in their approach to number, and children arrive in Year 1 from very different starting points. A Dubai parent worried at this stage should ask the class teacher for one specific observation rather than booking anything.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme, lower primary
programmes.description: Place value, addition and subtraction strategies, the start of multiplicative thinking, measurement with standard units. This is where a genuine gap first becomes visible and where a small number of well-targeted sessions does the most work per dirham, because misconceptions are still single and identifiable.
programmes.countryNote: The most common Dubai referral at this stage is a child who was fine in Year 2 and stalled in Year 3, which is almost always the transition from counting strategies to recall and place-value reasoning. Four to six sessions on one strand typically settles it.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme, upper primary
programmes.description: Fractions, decimals and percentages as one connected idea, proportional reasoning, area and volume, data handling and early probability. Costs rise here because the content genuinely needs a teacher, and because a gap left from Year 3 now shows up in four different topics at once.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai families often start spending in Year 6, driven by the move to the Middle Years Programme or to a British Year 7. That is late but not too late; six to ten sessions on fractions and proportional reasoning is the highest-value block available at primary age.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme mathematics
programmes.description: Criterion-referenced marking out of eight, a split into standard and extended routes around Year 10, and a jump in the amount of reasoning students must write down. Primary gaps that were invisible become expensive here, which is the honest financial case for spending something in Year 5 or 6.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the Year 7 intake at continuum schools mixes children from several primary systems, and teachers spend the first term finding gaps. A child who arrives fluent in number facts and comfortable with fractions is rarely the one who needs paid support in Year 8.

dubai/ib-pyp-maths-tutor.subjectsIntro: Primary maths is not one subject, and the cost of fixing a problem depends entirely on which part of it is broken. These are the areas we work on, with how quickly each one responds and therefore what it costs.

subjects.name: Number sense and place value
subjects.description: Understanding what the digits mean, not just reading them. A child who cannot say what happens to 304 when you take ten away has a place-value gap, and it will surface again in subtraction, decimals and rounding. Responds fast: three or four sessions plus short daily practice.

subjects.name: Addition and subtraction strategies
subjects.description: Bridging ten, compensation, partitioning, and subtracting across a zero. Most Dubai referrals at this age are here. The cheapest fix is usually a method made explicit once and then practised at home for ten minutes a day, which is tutoring at its most cost-effective.

subjects.name: Multiplication, division and number facts
subjects.description: Recall and the reasoning behind it. Fluency is a practice problem rather than a teaching problem, so paying an adult AED 200 an hour to drill tables is poor value. A tutor is worth it for the structure, division with remainders, and the link to fractions.

subjects.name: Fractions, decimals and percentages
subjects.description: The single highest-value strand to buy help with at primary age, because the three are one idea and most children are taught them as three. A gap here is the most reliable predictor of struggle in the first year of the Middle Years Programme. Expect six to ten sessions.

subjects.name: Pattern and function
subjects.description: Early algebra: sequences, rules, relationships, the unknown as a quantity rather than a missing box. Slowest strand to move and the one most dependent on a teacher spotting the misconception, which makes it the strand where a cheap tutor is a false economy.

subjects.name: Measurement
subjects.description: Standard units, conversion, perimeter, area, volume, time. Conversion errors in Dubai classrooms often come from mixed exposure to metric and imperial at home. Usually quick to fix and a good first strand for a family testing whether tutoring helps at all.

subjects.name: Shape and space
subjects.description: Properties, angles, symmetry, position and transformation. Visual and often a strength for children who struggle elsewhere, which makes it useful early in a block for rebuilding a child's belief that they can do mathematics.

subjects.name: Data handling and probability
subjects.description: Reading and making graphs, averages, early chance. Cheap to fix and frequently the strand where a child loses marks in an entrance assessment despite understanding the maths, because the question is about reading the axis rather than calculating.

subjects.name: Mathematical language and word problems
subjects.description: Turning sentences into operations. For Dubai's large population of children learning in English as an additional language, this is frequently the real problem being misread as a maths problem, and it needs a tutor who can tell the difference.

subjects.name: Mental calculation fluency
subjects.description: Speed and confidence with facts held in memory. The clearest case in all of primary maths for an app or a parent with flashcards rather than a paid hour. We will say so in the first lesson if that is what the diagnosis shows.

dubai/ib-pyp-maths-tutor.regionsTitle: Dubai communities, the four o'clock problem and what it costs
dubai/ib-pyp-maths-tutor.regionsIntro: For a primary-age child the binding constraint is not money, it is the half-hour window between getting home and losing the ability to concentrate. These notes cover when that window falls in different parts of Dubai, and what it means for what you pay.

regions.name: Dubai Hills Estate
regions.note: Short school runs for families whose children attend nearby, so a 3.45pm session is realistic and a young child is still fresh. That matters financially: a 25-minute session that lands in the good window achieves more than a bought hour at 6pm, at roughly half the cost.

regions.name: Al Barsha and Al Barsha South
regions.note: Dense school provision and generally short journeys, but heavy after-school club participation. Families here often find Thursday the only clear day, and a single longer weekly session on one strand is the sensible purchase rather than two scattered slots.

regions.name: Jumeirah Golf Estates and Dubai Sports City
regions.note: Training schedules dominate the late afternoon for many children. A morning weekend slot is usually better value than a weekday evening, because a tired seven-year-old at 6.30pm produces almost nothing a parent is paying for.

regions.name: Al Khawaneej and Mirdif
regions.note: Longer journeys from central Dubai schools, which pushes the window past 5pm and makes short sessions essential rather than optional. Online delivery removes the tutor's travel from the equation entirely, which is where the in-home premium mostly goes.

regions.name: Business Bay and Downtown Dubai
regions.note: Apartment living with working parents nearby, so a parent can often attend the first session without taking leave. Worth doing once for a primary child, because what you are really assessing is whether the tutor can hold a nine-year-old's attention.

regions.name: Mudon, Town Square and Dubailand
regions.note: Younger families with several children close in age, which makes the sibling-sharing question live. Our honest answer is in the table below: it halves the rate and halves the value, and two separate 25-minute slots usually cost the same as one shared hour.

regions.name: Dubai Creek Harbour and Al Jaddaf
regions.note: Newer communities with a high proportion of families recently arrived in the PYP. First-year parents here spend most on tutoring and need it least; a term of reading the school's own reporting usually answers the question for free.

regions.name: Dubai South and The Sustainable City
regions.note: Longer distances and limited local tutor supply, which is where an in-home arrangement becomes both expensive and unreliable. One-to-one live video costs the same here as in Jumeirah, which is the clearest practical case for the format.

schoolClusters.city: Central and western Dubai primary provision
schoolClusters.note: Students we support in these communities are usually at schools with established PYP maths practice and good intervention groups, which means the free option should be tried first. Where families still come to us it is most often for fractions in Years 5 and 6, or for a specific place-value gap identified by the class teacher.

schoolClusters.city: Eastern and southern Dubai primary provision
schoolClusters.note: A wider spread of curricula, and more children moving between systems mid-primary. Students we support from these areas more often need the mathematical language work rather than the mathematics, because a change of system changes the vocabulary of the questions before it changes the content.

sections.heading: What a Dubai maths hour buys at each published price point
paragraphs: The published rate ladder in this emirate is wide and badly explained, so here it is with what each rung actually delivers for a primary child. At the bottom, EdFlik advertises online tuition from AED 45 to AED 65 per hour and Tutopiya from roughly AED 33 to AED 52, generally using university students and recent graduates. In the middle, Unitors publishes IGCSE tuition from AED 150 and IB tuition from AED 200. TutorChase lists AED 270 per hour for specialist support. Bestimate's Dubai rate survey reports in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to AED 350 and specialist exam-year help at AED 200 to AED 450 and above, with BartyED advertising AED 650 for premium named tutors. Those are other providers' published figures, read in October 2026, and none of them are IB Gram prices.

For a nine-year-old with a place-value gap, the difference between the rungs is diagnostic skill rather than subject knowledge. Everyone on that ladder can do primary arithmetic. Not everyone can watch a child subtract 304 minus 10, see that they are counting back rather than reasoning about the tens digit, and know which of four possible misconceptions is in play. That is a trained primary teacher's skill and it is the whole value proposition at the upper rates. A cheaper tutor will reteach the method the school already taught, which the child will follow in the session and fail at again on Tuesday.

The honest arithmetic follows from that. Six sessions at AED 200 that fix a misconception cost AED 1,200 and end. Twenty sessions at AED 50 that supervise homework cost AED 1,000 and do not end, because nothing was diagnosed. The cost per hour favours the second and the cost per fixed problem favours the first by a wide margin. The exception is genuine: if the problem is purely fluency, the cheap tutor and the expensive tutor are equally unnecessary and a free app with a parent checking it beats both.

sections.heading: Costing it by strand: the five parts of PYP maths do not cost the same
paragraphs: PYP mathematics is organised into five strands: number, pattern and function, measurement, shape and space, and data handling. Buying tutoring without knowing which strand is broken is how Dubai families end up twelve sessions in with a child who is still stuck, because the sessions have been covering the strand that was never the problem.

The strands respond at very different speeds and therefore cost very different amounts to fix. Measurement conversion errors and data-handling misreadings are usually two or three sessions. A place-value gap is three or four, plus daily practice. Fractions, decimals and percentages treated as one connected idea is six to ten, and it is the best money anyone spends at primary age because it is the strongest predictor of difficulty in the first Middle Years year. Pattern and function is the slowest and the most teacher-dependent, because the misconceptions are conceptual rather than procedural.

What this means practically is that you should buy one strand. Not a term of maths, not general support, one strand, with an agreed end point. Our session notes name the strand and the specific misconception being addressed, which is what lets a parent see that the money is going where they decided it should. A provider who cannot tell you which strand they are working on this week is selling hours rather than teaching. The table below applies the mid-market figure of AED 200 an hour, which is where Unitors' published IB rate starts, to each strand. Read it as arithmetic on somebody else's quoted rate rather than as our price list, and use it to sanity-check any quote you are given, including ours.

sections.heading: The cheaper options, costed honestly
paragraphs: A tutoring page that never recommends not buying tutoring is advertising. There are four cheaper options for a Dubai primary maths worry and at least two of them are better than a paid hour for the most common problems. They are listed below with real costs and real limits, and we will point a family at any of them in the free first lesson if the diagnosis says so.

The school's own intervention group is first for a reason. It costs nothing, it is run by someone who sees your child every day, and KHDA-inspected schools in Dubai generally have a functioning referral process. The thing to ask for is specific: not extra help, but which strand the school thinks is weak and what the intervention will target. A school that cannot answer that is a reason to look outside; a school that answers it well has just done your diagnosis for free.

Fluency apps are second, and genuinely effective for the single most common primary complaint. If the problem is that a child knows how to multiply but is slow and loses confidence, ten minutes a day on a structured practice app for a few dirhams a month will do more than an adult at AED 200 an hour. The honest limit is that an app cannot find a misconception; it will drill a wrong method as cheerfully as a right one. That is exactly where a single diagnostic session earns its keep and a block of twenty does not.

sections.heading: Where Dubai families actually waste money on primary maths
paragraphs: Four patterns account for most of the wasted spending we see, and none of them are about choosing a bad tutor. The first is buying a term. A term is a unit of school administration, not a unit of teaching, and a child with a measurement gap needs three sessions rather than twelve. Providers sell terms because terms are predictable revenue. Families buy them because the alternative requires a diagnosis nobody offered.

The second is paying an adult to drill. Number-fact fluency is a repetition problem and repetition is the cheapest commodity in education. Watching a tutor at AED 200 an hour run times tables with a nine-year-old is the clearest waste in this market, and it is extremely common because it looks like work and the child does get faster. They would have got faster for free.

The third is starting too early. A worried parent of a five-year-old is usually responding to a developmental range rather than a problem, and paid intervention at that age mostly buys the parent reassurance. The fourth is starting too late in a different sense: leaving a fractions gap from Year 5 until the second term of Year 7, by which point it is showing up across four topics and costs three times as much to close. Spending in Year 6 is the single best-timed primary purchase in Dubai, and spending in Year 1 is usually the worst. A fifth pattern deserves a mention because it is invisible to the family paying for it: booking the only slot left rather than the right one. A nine-year-old at 6.30pm after a long school run produces perhaps ten useful minutes, whatever the tutor charges for the hour.

sections.heading: Why the PYP report has no percentage, and how to read it for spending decisions
paragraphs: Dubai parents who grew up with marks out of a hundred find PYP reporting genuinely hard to act on. There are no examinations and no percentages. Reporting describes what a child can do against learning outcomes and conceptual understandings, often in sentences that sound uniformly positive. A report saying a child is developing an understanding of fractions could describe a child two months behind or a child comfortably on track, and the sentence is identical.

The way to extract a spending decision from it is to ask three specific questions at the next parent meeting, in writing if necessary. Which of the five strands is weakest for my child. What specifically does she do when she gets a question in that strand wrong. And what is the school already doing about it. A teacher who sees your child daily can answer all three in five minutes, and the answers are a better diagnosis than any paid assessment, because they are based on months of observation rather than one session.

Those answers also change what you should buy. If the teacher says the strand is number and the error is counting back rather than reasoning about place value, that is three or four sessions on one thing. If the teacher says the maths is fine but the child cannot get started on a word problem, the issue is mathematical language, which is a different tutor and often a different subject entirely. If the teacher cannot name a strand or an error, that is itself information, and a single diagnostic session is then worth more than a term of anything.

sections.heading: Transdisciplinary maths, and why the homework looks nothing like yours
paragraphs: In the PYP, a good deal of mathematics is taught inside units of inquiry rather than as a separate subject, with stand-alone teaching alongside it. So a Dubai parent may see their Year 4 child measuring shadows for a unit about light and conclude that no mathematics is being taught. Measurement, data handling and often shape and space are being taught, in a context the child will remember. What is harder to see from outside is whether the underlying number work is being practised to fluency.

That design has a practical consequence for tutoring. A tutor who ignores the school's units and runs a parallel curriculum confuses the child and wastes the connection the school has built. A tutor who works only inside the units never gets to the fluency practice that transdisciplinary teaching does not naturally provide. The useful arrangement is a tutor who asks what the current unit is, uses its context where it fits, and does the number work separately and explicitly.

It also affects how a parent reads progress. Mathematics that appears in a unit of inquiry is assessed in the context of that unit, so a child can look confident in the measuring task and still be shaky on conversion in isolation. Asking a child to do the same operation out of context is a cheap and reliable test that any parent can run, and it frequently explains a mismatch between a warm school report and a struggle with homework.

sections.heading: What the spend is actually buying later: Checkpoint, MYP and the Year 7 step
paragraphs: The financial case for primary maths spending is not about Year 4. It is about what a gap costs later, and the costs are very unevenly distributed across the strands. A measurement gap in Year 4 is a measurement gap in Year 7, closed in two sessions whenever anyone notices. A fractions gap in Year 5 becomes, by Year 8, a problem in ratio, algebra, probability and percentage change simultaneously, and closing it then takes three times as long because four topics have to be revisited.

Some Dubai schools also use Cambridge Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests, which Cambridge International runs in March, May and October. Where a school uses them, they are a useful external reading in a programme that otherwise provides none, and worth asking about rather than worrying about. They are diagnostic rather than high-stakes, and no tutoring is required to sit them.

The step into Middle Years mathematics is where primary spending either pays or does not. The programme marks against four criteria out of eight and asks students to write reasoning down, which primary rarely demands. A child who arrives fluent in number facts, comfortable converting between fractions, decimals and percentages, and used to showing a method will handle the transition. That is a short, specific list, and it is exactly what a well-targeted Year 6 block should be built around rather than general confidence. Families moving instead to a British Year 7 in Dubai face a similar but shorter list, since written method and fluency matter there too and the fractions work is identical. Either way, the target is three or four specific capabilities rather than a general sense that the child is ready.

sections.heading: Home tutoring for a primary child in Dubai, and the honest trade
paragraphs: The case for a visiting tutor is strongest at primary age and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. A six-year-old works better with an adult physically beside them, concrete materials on the table, and no screen to look away from. The Dubai market serves this: Bestimate's survey reports in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to AED 350 per hour, with monthly in-home packages of AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour sessions in circulation. Those are other providers' published figures with their reading date.

IB Gram does not run home visits in Dubai or anywhere in the UAE. Visiting tutors are a service we operate only in India, and we would rather say that plainly than take a booking and explain later. For every UAE family lessons are one-to-one on live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time. Two honest points in favour: the travel premium disappears from the hour, and a 25-minute session becomes practical, which for a seven-year-old is the right length and is not economic for a tutor who has driven across Dubai to deliver it.

The genuine limits are worth stating. A child under about six is a poor fit for video, and we will say so rather than take the booking. A child who needs physical manipulatives can use household objects with a parent nearby for the first few sessions, which works but asks something of the parent. And a child who will not engage with a screen without an adult present is a real case for in-home, which we do not provide in this market.
