sections.heading: Two children, two curricula, one quiet room
paragraphs: This is the most under-discussed constraint in tower living and the one families are most reluctant to raise. A two-bedroom flat in the JLT clusters has, realistically, one place where a child can work without being interrupted, and in many households it is also where somebody takes work calls. Two children cannot both use it at six o'clock, and a tutoring plan that assumes otherwise falls apart quietly.

The arrangements that hold are unglamorous. Stagger the slots rather than stacking them: one child at 6.30pm and the other at 7.30pm, rather than both at the same time in different rooms. Give the child in a session the room with the door, and the child doing silent revision the kitchen table with headphones. Use a headset with a microphone rather than a laptop speaker, which stops the tutor hearing the room and stops the room hearing the tutor.

Exam season makes it worse, because the two seasons do not coincide. The February and March window for Indian-curriculum board exams is the British-curriculum child's mid-year, and the May and June IGCSE window is the Indian-curriculum child's new academic year. For roughly four months a year one child is in a critical period while the other is in ordinary term time, and priority for the quiet room has to be decided openly rather than fought over nightly.

There is a positive side worth naming. A household that has already negotiated two calendars and two systems tends to be unusually good at logistics by the time the older child reaches a Diploma or A Level, and the younger child benefits from parents who have learned to ask schools precise questions. The skill transfers; the floor space does not.

sections.heading: Why the fee decision put your children in different systems, and what to do about it
paragraphs: Very few JLT families chose two curricula on educational grounds. The usual sequence is that the first child was placed where a seat and a fee level coincided, the second child's needs or the household's finances changed, and the result is two systems. There is no reason to be apologetic about that, and there is good reason to manage it deliberately rather than pretending both children are in the same race.

The first management step is to stop comparing marks. A percentage from one board and a grade from another are not comparable, and a tier decision sitting behind one of them makes the comparison worse. Replace the comparison with two separate questions: is this child progressing against their own last report, and is this child entered for the thing that keeps their next step open?

The second is to understand that the exit routes differ. For Ministry of Education equivalency, the British track requires five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from the five, plus one accredited Advanced Level subject at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. A family with children on two different tracks has two different document requirements, and discovering that in the month a certificate is needed is the avoidable version of this problem.

The third is to make a decision about convergence. Some households deliberately bring the second child onto the first child's system at a natural break — the end of Class 8, or after Class 10 into a sixth form — which costs money and simplifies everything thereafter. Others keep both and manage it. Both are legitimate; what causes trouble is drifting without deciding, and then finding at 15 that an option block in one school and a board timetable in the other have made the decision for you.

sections.heading: What tutoring costs for a JLT household, including the second child
paragraphs: Published market rates in this corridor run from roughly AED 33 an hour to above AED 600, and the spread is explained by what the hour contains rather than by local differences. Tutopiya advertises from AED 33 to 52 and EdFlik from AED 45 to 65, which buys a generalist or a university student. Unitors publishes IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200 for a qualified subject tutor online. Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table puts exam-year specialist support at AED 200 to 450 or above, TutorChase lists AED 270, and BartyED lists AED 650 for a premium named tutor.

For a household buying for two children the arithmetic deserves care, because the temptation is to find one tutor who will take both. That is usually a false economy in a two-board household: a tutor fluent in Cambridge 0580 teaching a CBSE Class 10 sibling is working outside their syllabus, and the second child receives generic mathematics rather than board-specific preparation. Two specialists at a sensible rate beats one generalist at a discount.

In-home visits are priced with travel inside them — Bestimate puts them at AED 180 to 350, with independents quoting to AED 500 — and in the JLT clusters a tutor arriving at seven faces the same tower-access reality as any visitor. Monthly packages seen in the market include AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions; Bestimate's monthly estimates for a weekly hour are AED 240 to 600 at the budget tier, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-range and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support.

All of those are other people's published figures, read in October 2026, and they are the market rather than our price. IB Gram quotes after a free trial lesson, per child and per subject, with the scope written down. Where a household is buying for two children we will say plainly if one of them does not currently need anything, because selling a second seat to a family under pressure is the easiest unnecessary sale in this market.

sections.heading: A tutor in the flat against one-to-one online, for this household
paragraphs: Families in the clusters do look for an in-home tutor, and the honest answer is that it exists, costs more, and brings overhead a working household feels disproportionately. Bestimate's Dubai figures put in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350 an hour with independents quoting to AED 500, and in a JLT tower a visitor at seven in the evening involves access, parking and a lift in a building designed around office hours.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Lessons here are one-to-one over live video. For a two-board household the decisive argument is matching: each child needs a tutor who knows their own board, and in a community with no school inside it, the chance that two such specialists both live within driving distance and are free on the same evening is small.

The second argument is the hidden labour already described. A video session removes the door, the settling and the supervision from a parent's evening and replaces them with a written note they can read later. For a household where both adults work nearby and late, that is not a convenience, it is the difference between an arrangement that lasts a year and one that lasts a month.

The third is turnover. JLT is a transient community by design, and families move between clusters, to another emirate, or out of the UAE on short cycles. A tutor relationship built over video survives all three, which matters most for a student mid-course whose predicted grades will be written by whoever is teaching them next year.

sections.heading: Is your tutor legally permitted to teach in the UAE?
paragraphs: A household paying two tutors is entitled to ask about permits, and the position is clear and public. The MoHRE private tutor work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 Regarding the Introduction of Private Tuition Work Permits. It is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18, and university students.

Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit from MoHRE are subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published — Khaleej Times reported that the ministry did not specify the fine amounts or detail the penalties — so a figure circulating online cannot be sourced to anyone. MoHRE's own service page is titled Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time, and is used through the MoHRE smart app, website and e-services system.

There is a separate rule that matters in a household with two schools, and it is frequently misunderstood. Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with their own school. That reporting should be verified against the current ADEK policy document before anyone relies on exact wording, but the practical instruction is simple: do not arrange for either child's own teacher to tutor them privately.

A tutoring business with premises and staff in Dubai is a different legal animal again. It needs a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute, with initial approval first, a maximum of six months to complete the permit and licence steps, and annual renewal requested at least 30 days before expiry. IB Gram holds no such permit, runs no UAE premises, and claims no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, MoHRE, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson.

sections.heading: Starting from a JLT address, with two calendars to respect
paragraphs: The first message that helps names both children: school, year group, subjects, and board or syllabus code where known. If codes are unknown, the useful action is two emails rather than one — each child's exams officer, asked for the syllabus code, tier and series in writing. Departments inside one school sometimes differ, and the two schools certainly do.

Then two free trial lessons rather than one, because two children on two boards need two specialists. Each is a real lesson with a diagnostic purpose, with no card details taken and no commitment. Afterwards you get two written views in the same format, which is the first time most two-board households have been able to compare their children's positions on comparable terms.

On scheduling, tell us the constraints rather than the preferences: which bus returns when, which room is available, and which evenings a parent is reliably home. We will build the slots around those and stagger them so the quiet room is needed once per evening. Late slots are normal here and sessions can shift to post-Iftar times through Ramadan.

Finally, expect to be told when one child does not need anything. In a household already paying for one child, adding the second is the easiest sale in this market and often the wrong one. If the honest answer is a two-session parent board-literacy block and nothing else for the younger child, that is what we will quote for.

process.title: Tell us about both children at once
process.description: School, year group, subjects and board for each child, with syllabus codes where you have them. A two-board household is a single scheduling problem and two separate teaching problems, and treating it that way from the first message avoids the common outcome where one child is organised properly and the other is handled as an afterthought.

process.title: Two emails to two exams officers
process.description: For each child, ask the exams officer in writing for the syllabus code, the tier and the series for every subject. For the Cambridge child in particular, the tier is the question nobody volunteers, and a Core entry caps the grade at 5 in most subjects. For the Indian-curriculum child, confirm the board exam calendar for the year ahead.

process.title: A free trial for each child, with their own specialist
process.description: Two trial lessons rather than one, each with the tutor who would actually teach that child's board. No card details, no commitment. We deliberately do not offer one tutor to cover both children, because a Cambridge specialist teaching a CBSE sibling is working outside their syllabus and the second child gets generic help.

process.title: Two written views, in one format
process.description: After the trials you get a view on each child in identical format: what needs weekly work, what needs a finite block, and what needs nothing. For most two-board households this is the first genuinely comparable picture of both children they have had, because the schools report in incompatible instruments.

process.title: Slots built around buses, rooms and working hours
process.description: We schedule from your constraints: which bus returns when, which room is free, which evenings an adult is home. Slots are staggered so the flat's quiet room is occupied once per evening, and late starts are normal in this community. Sessions move by half an hour when an evening goes wrong rather than being cancelled.

process.title: Reviewed each half term, both children at once
process.description: Every half term we look at both children together and say where the budget should sit. Sometimes that means moving hours from one child to the other, sometimes dropping a subject because the gap closed, and sometimes stopping for one child entirely. A household should not be paying twice out of symmetry.

We keep both on one view, including entry deadlines, because the collisions are predictable and the surprises are not.

faqs.question: Is there a secondary school inside JLT?
faqs.answer: No. The JLT clusters contain nurseries and early-years provision but no secondary school, so every older child commutes out — most often to The Greens, Jumeirah Village, Emirates Living, Al Barsha or the Jebel Ali corridor. The practical effect is that households in neighbouring towers have children at different schools on different boards, so the usual shortcut of asking which tutor the building uses produces a poor answer here. The matching variable is the syllabus code rather than the address.

faqs.question: Our two children are on different curricula. Can one tutor cover both?
faqs.answer: Technically yes and usually it is a false economy. A tutor fluent in Cambridge 0580 teaching a CBSE Class 10 sibling is working outside their own syllabus, and the second child receives generic mathematics rather than board-specific preparation for the paper they will actually sit. Two specialists at sensible rates beats one generalist at a discount, and we quote it that way deliberately. The one thing genuinely worth buying jointly is a short session for the parents on what each board's reporting actually measures.

faqs.question: How do I compare a CBSE percentage with an IGCSE grade?
faqs.answer: You cannot, and nobody should offer you a table that does. IGCSE grade boundaries are set per paper per series after marking, precisely so that variation in paper difficulty can be accounted for, which means no fixed relationship between a percentage and a grade exists even within one board. The useful substitute is two separate questions per child: are they progressing against their own last report, and are they entered for something that keeps their next step open? Those are answerable; the comparison is not.

faqs.question: What is tiering, and why has nobody mentioned it to me?
faqs.answer: Most Cambridge IGCSE subjects split into Core and Extended papers covering different amounts of the same syllabus, and Core caps the achievable grade at 5. The school decides which tier a child is entered at, subject by subject, and the decision is effectively fixed once final entries are submitted. Parents arriving from systems with no tiering — CBSE and ICSE have none — do not think to ask, and schools rarely volunteer it. Ask the exams officer for the tier per subject in writing, in October at the latest.

faqs.question: Our two children's exam seasons fall at different times of year. How do we plan around that?
faqs.answer: Accept that for about four months a year one child is in a critical window while the other is in ordinary term time, and decide priorities openly rather than nightly. Indian-curriculum board exams fall in February and March on an April-to-March year; IGCSE papers fall in May and June on a September-to-July year. That means the quiet room, the family calendar and parental attention have two peak seasons. Families who write both calendars onto one view in September argue far less in February.

faqs.question: What time should a session start for a child on the Jumeirah Village bus run?
faqs.answer: Plan for 6.30pm or later. That run is long rather than slow, crosses Al Khail Road, and typically returns a child hungry well after 4.30pm. In this community a session kept every week at 7pm is worth more than one scheduled at 5pm and cancelled twice a month, and attention with food inside a child at 7.30pm is usually better than attention at 5pm without. Online slots can also shift by half an hour on a bad evening instead of being lost entirely.

faqs.question: Both parents work nearby and get home late. Does that make tutoring harder?
faqs.answer: It makes in-home tutoring harder and online tutoring largely unaffected. Every visiting arrangement carries hidden adult labour — admitting someone, settling the child, keeping a sibling out, taking the handover at the door — and in a two-working-parent household that is what causes arrangements to fail in week three. A video session at an agreed time needs nobody home, and a written note afterwards lets a parent engage at nine o'clock with what was covered and what was set.

faqs.question: We only have one quiet room. Can two children both have lessons?
faqs.answer: Yes, by staggering rather than stacking. One child at 6.30pm and the other at 7.30pm works far better than both at once in different corners of a two-bedroom flat. Give the child in a session the room with the door, let the other work at the kitchen table with headphones, and use a headset with a microphone rather than a laptop speaker so neither the tutor nor the room is competing with the other. Tell us the constraint at the start; it changes which slots we offer.

faqs.question: Which subjects do JLT families most often ask about?
faqs.answer: Mathematics first by a wide margin, across every board, followed by Chemistry and Physics at IGCSE and Higher Level mathematics in the Diploma. Among Indian-curriculum siblings the pattern shifts towards Class 10 Mathematics and Science ahead of the board exams. The subject families underestimate is English: IGCSE directed writing and the Diploma's individual oral both reward apparatus that is taught in class and practised almost nowhere, and a strong report in English rarely predicts performance in either.

faqs.question: Do tutors come to the JLT towers, or are the lessons online?
faqs.answer: Online. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. In-home tutoring does exist in Dubai, with published rates of AED 180 to 350 an hour and independents quoting to AED 500, and in a JLT tower a visitor at seven in the evening deals with access, parking and a lift in a building built around office hours. For a two-board household the decisive point is that each child needs a tutor matched to their own syllabus, which is not a geographic search.

faqs.question: What do tutors charge in this part of Dubai right now?
faqs.answer: Published figures as of October 2026: Tutopiya advertises from AED 33 to 52 an hour and EdFlik from AED 45 to 65 at the generalist end; Unitors publishes IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200 for a qualified subject tutor online; TutorChase lists AED 270 and BartyED AED 650 at the specialist and premium end. Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table puts in-home visits at AED 180 to 350 and exam-year specialists at AED 200 to 450 or above. Those are their figures; we quote after a free trial.

faqs.question: Should we move the younger child onto the same curriculum as the older one?
faqs.answer: It is a legitimate decision and the point to take it is a natural break: the end of Class 8 into Year 9, or after Class 10 into a sixth form. Converging costs money and simplifies everything afterwards — one calendar, one reporting instrument, one set of entry deadlines. Keeping both systems is equally legitimate if managed deliberately. What causes trouble is drifting, then discovering at 15 that an option block in one school and a board timetable in the other have made the decision for you.

faqs.question: Do my children need different documents for UAE equivalency?
faqs.answer: Probably, because the requirements differ by track. The published British track asks for five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education not counted among the five, plus one accredited Advanced Level subject at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. For an Indian-curriculum certificate, verify the requirement with the Ministry of Education or your emirate's attestation authority. IB Gram does not perform or guarantee any part of that process.

faqs.question: Does our tutor need a UAE permit, and can we check it?
faqs.answer: They need the MoHRE private tutor work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, which is granted free of charge for two years and open to school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Applications go through the MoHRE smart app, website and e-services system under the service name Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, with a two-working-day completion time. Tutoring without one attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws, though no fine schedule is published.

faqs.question: Can one of my children's own school teachers tutor them privately?
faqs.answer: Not for payment where the child is enrolled at that teacher's school. Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with their own school. That reporting should be checked against the current ADEK policy document before anyone relies on the exact wording, but the practical position is unambiguous: use an independent tutor rather than your child's own teacher, in either school.

faqs.question: Can sessions continue when we travel or if we move out of JLT?
faqs.answer: Yes, which is one of the quieter advantages of a video arrangement in a transient community. Families in the clusters move between towers, to another emirate, or out of the UAE on short cycles, and a tutor relationship survives all three unchanged. During travel, sessions either pause or continue at whatever hour the destination timezone allows. Through Ramadan slots commonly move to a post-Iftar time, which works considerably better online than it does with a visitor crossing the city late in the evening.

dubai/jlt.closingHeading: One household, two systems, two specialists
dubai/jlt.closingBody: If you are in the JLT clusters running two curricula at once, the most useful thing you can do this week is send two emails: one to each child's exams officer, asking for the syllabus code, the tier and the series in writing. Send us what comes back and two free trial lessons follow, one per child with their own board specialist, delivered live online in slots built around your bus times and your working hours. You will get two written views in the same format — including, where it is true, the one that says this child needs nothing right now.

intro.heading: Who lives in Jumeirah 1, and why the Arabic question lands here first
paragraphs: Jumeirah 1 is the oldest of the coastal residential districts, running between Al Wasl Road and the beach, anchored by Jumeirah Mosque, Mercato, the Iranian Hospital and the villa streets behind 2nd of December Street. It is a low-rise, long-settled area, and its population mix is distinct from the newer coastal communities to the south: a higher proportion of Emirati households, a large Arab expatriate community, and long-tenured international families who have lived in Dubai for a decade or more rather than two years.

That mix changes the academic question a parent brings. In a newly built apartment community the question is usually which school and is my child behind. Here, families are generally settled in a school and the live question is about balance: how a child carries nine or ten IGCSE subjects, or six Diploma subjects, alongside Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies that are mandatory in every Dubai private school regardless of the licensed international curriculum.

This is the part of the UAE market almost nobody writes about. Across the competitor pages ranking for Dubai tutoring queries, Arabic appears as a subject chip and Islamic Education and Social Studies barely appear at all. Yet KHDA's requirements are detailed and specific, and the consequences for a family are real. These subjects occupy timetable hours, they are reported on, and for an Arabic-first student the standard is genuinely demanding because it is taught as a first language, not as an acquisition subject.

The second thing that marks out Jumeirah 1 is destination. A significant share of students in this district are aiming at UAE universities as a first or serious option, which means the Ministry of Education equivalency route matters to them in a way it does not to a family whose child will apply only to the United Kingdom. Equivalency has specific, published subject and grade requirements on the British and American tracks, and getting them wrong in Year 10 is an expensive mistake to discover in Year 13.

The schools themselves are close. Emirates International School Jumeirah runs the IB continuum on Jumeirah Beach Road. Al Ittihad Private School Jumeira and JSS Private School sit within the district. Latifa School for Girls has been part of this area for decades. Immediately south in Al Safa are Jumeirah College, Jumeirah Primary School, Jumeira Baccalaureate School and Horizon English School, and Dubai Japanese School is in Al Wasl. For most Jumeirah 1 addresses the school run is short by Dubai standards, and the beach-road traffic rather than the distance is the constraint.

Everything described here is delivered as one-to-one tuition over live video. IB Gram does not send tutors to addresses in the UAE; home visits are a service we provide only in India. For Arabic and Islamic Education in particular, online matching matters more than it might appear: the pool of tutors qualified to teach Arabic as a first language at secondary level is not large, and restricting it to people who can drive to Jumeirah 1 on a Tuesday evening makes it smaller still.

dubai/jumeirah-1.programmesIntro: Jumeirah 1 families are usually choosing how to combine an international programme with the UAE's mandatory subjects, and each programme makes that combination differently.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: Nine or ten examined subjects over two years. Arabic and Islamic Education sit alongside the examined timetable as school-assessed mandatory provision in Dubai, which means a Year 10 student here has a fuller week than the subject count alone suggests. Tier choices in mathematics and the sciences cap or open the grades available.
programmes.countryNote: For Ministry of Education equivalency on the British track, five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than E or grade 3 are required, and Arabic and Islamic Education are not included among those five. One ranking competitor states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects. The sourced figure is five. Verify the current requirement on the authority's own page before planning around it.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects across three Higher and three Standard Levels, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Arabic-first students often take Arabic as a Group 1 language and literature subject, which is a different and more demanding proposition than Arabic in Group 2, and it changes what tutoring is useful.
programmes.countryNote: No IB points threshold for UAE equivalency should be taken second-hand. The published equivalency guidance covers the British and American tracks in detail; the IB figure has not been read on a Ministry page and this site therefore does not publish one. Ask the attestation authority directly rather than relying on a figure quoted in a tutoring advertisement.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Four criteria per subject, each out of eight, converted through published boundaries. Language and literature in Arabic is available as a first-language option in MYP at schools that offer it, and for Arabic-first families this is the stage where a decision quietly gets made about whether Arabic remains a first language into the Diploma.
programmes.countryNote: Emirates International School Jumeirah runs the IB continuum within the district, which makes the MYP a realistic local option rather than a theoretical one. Families should ask specifically which language streams are offered at which levels, because the availability of Arabic language and literature varies between campuses.

programmes.name: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies
programmes.ageRange: All year groups, all Dubai private schools
programmes.description: Mandatory in every Dubai private school whatever the licensed international curriculum. KHDA requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, because curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ between the groups, and combined classes are prohibited.
programmes.countryNote: KHDA calculates mandatory-subject instructional time on a forty-minute lesson unit, allows schools to vary lesson length provided total weekly time is met, and advises that any mandatory-subject lesson should be at least twenty-five minutes. Schools must also ensure teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate KHDA approval for those subjects.

dubai/jumeirah-1.subjectsIntro: Jumeirah 1 households ask for a mix other districts do not. These are the subjects most requested here, including the mandatory streams that run alongside the international curriculum.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first language
subjects.levels: Primary and secondary · MYP and IB Group 1
subjects.description: Taught in Standard Arabic with first-language expectations for grammar, classical and modern literature, and extended writing. Students from Arabic-speaking homes who are fluent in dialect frequently struggle with the formal register, which is a teachable gap rather than a language problem.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: A separate course with separate expectations, covering reading, listening, speaking and writing at an acquisition level. KHDA requires it to be taught in classes separate from the first-language stream because the curriculum expectations differ.

subjects.name: Islamic Education
subjects.description: Mandatory provision with two streams. For Arab students the language of instruction is Standard Arabic; for non-Arab students it is the school's licensed-curriculum language. Memorisation, text handling and written response are the usual areas where support is sought.

subjects.name: UAE Social Studies and Moral Education
subjects.description: Covers UAE history, geography, civics and national identity, taught in Arabic for Arab students and in the school's curriculum language for non-Arabs. Assessment rewards accurate recall of specific content, so targeted revision is unusually effective here.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Proof and calculus carry the examined papers. Students in a full timetable with mandatory subjects on top often need the exploration scheduled earlier than their peers, because their free periods are genuinely fewer.

subjects.name: IGCSE Mathematics
subjects.description: The tier decision governs the ceiling. Extended and Higher tier add algebraic fractions, circle theorems and function transformations that the lower tiers never assess, and the choice is usually made in Year 9 on Year 9 evidence.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL · IGCSE 0620 and 4CH1
subjects.description: Mole calculations and organic chemistry decide the grade. At Diploma level the internal assessment needs a research question narrow enough to control with school equipment, which is a design problem before it is a chemistry problem.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL · IGCSE 0625 and 4PH1
subjects.description: Explanation questions asking for a mechanism rather than an equation are where marks go. Electricity and circuits is the reliable IGCSE weak point; at Higher Level it is fields and the mathematics underneath them.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL · IGCSE 0610 and 4BI1
subjects.description: Command terms are the hidden syllabus, and data-response questions reward reading axes and units before answering. Content knowledge is rarely the limiting factor at either level.

subjects.name: English Language and Literature
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL · IGCSE First Language English
subjects.description: For bilingual students the written register is the usual target rather than comprehension. IGCSE directed writing marks turn on audience and register, and the Diploma Higher Level essay rewards a sustained argument about how a text works.

subjects.name: Business Management and Economics
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL · IGCSE Business Studies
subjects.description: Application to the named case rather than general theory earns the marks. In Economics, diagram accuracy plus an explicit judgement sentence is what separates a mid-band answer from a top-band one.

sections.heading: The half of a Dubai timetable nobody writes about
paragraphs: Private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific national curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but they must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. That federal rule is the foundation under every emirate's mandatory-subject requirement, and in Dubai it is given detail by KHDA. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum.

For a Jumeirah 1 family this is not an abstraction. It means a student in a British or IB school is also carrying a second set of subjects, with their own standards, their own reporting and their own language of instruction, which for Arabic-first students and for Islamic Education for Arabs is Standard Arabic. Those subjects consume real timetable hours, which is why a Year 10 week here is fuller than a subject count implies, and why scheduling tuition for this district is a different conversation from scheduling it elsewhere.

KHDA's requirements are specific enough to be checkable. Schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and combined classes for both groups are prohibited because curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Instructional time is calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit; schools may vary lesson length provided total weekly time is met, and any mandatory-subject lesson is advised to run at least twenty-five minutes.

Two further rules shape what tutoring can usefully do. Schools are required to ensure that teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects. And for the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior Ministry permission is prohibited, which means a tutor working in these subjects supports the prescribed material rather than importing an alternative syllabus.

sections.heading: Arabic as a first language is a different course from Arabic as an acquisition subject
paragraphs: This distinction is the single most useful thing a Jumeirah 1 parent can understand about the Arabic half of the timetable, and it is routinely missed, including by families who speak Arabic at home. A child who is fluent in a spoken dialect is not therefore proficient in Standard Arabic, and the first-language course is assessed in Standard Arabic against first-language expectations: formal grammar, classical and modern literary texts, and sustained academic writing.

What this produces is a specific and very common pattern. A child who converses easily at home, who is told by relatives that their Arabic is excellent, comes home with a mediocre Arabic grade and nobody can explain why. The answer is almost always register and written accuracy rather than comprehension. It is a teachable gap, and it responds quickly when the teaching targets the written formal language rather than general practice.

The acquisition stream is a different course with different aims, and KHDA requires it to be taught in separate classes precisely because the expectations differ. For a non-Arab family the usual problem is the opposite one: no support is available at home, homework cannot be checked by a parent, and the subject drifts because it is nobody's priority until a report lands. Short, regular sessions work better here than long ones.

The decision point worth planning for arrives in the middle years. For a student heading into the Diploma, taking Arabic as a Group 1 language and literature subject is a serious commitment and a genuine asset; taking it in Group 2 is a different proposition. Which is right depends on the student's actual written Standard Arabic rather than on how they speak, and an honest assessment of that in MYP 4 saves a difficult conversation in Diploma Year 1.

sections.heading: Five regulators, one country: what changes when a family moves emirate
paragraphs: Jumeirah 1 households move within the UAE more often than they leave it, and the regulator changes when they do. This is the single most under-reported fact in this market: ADEK, Abu Dhabi's own education authority, is named by none of the competitor pages researched for this project, and SPEA appears once across an entire cluster. For a family considering a job move to Abu Dhabi or Sharjah, that absence is unhelpful.

The map is straightforward. In Dubai, the Knowledge and Human Development Authority is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. In Abu Dhabi and Al Ain, the Department of Education and Knowledge supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools. In Sharjah, the Sharjah Private Education Authority regulates private education, and in Ras Al Khaimah the Department of Knowledge does the same. The Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah.

The differences are not cosmetic. Sharjah's and Ras Al Khaimah's authorities approve tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods, so curriculum and fee approval sits with the emirate regulator rather than only inspection. Abu Dhabi's ADEK additionally sets professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff that bar teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school.

What a parent should take from this is practical. When you move emirate, the inspection framework, the fee approval process and the rules governing who may tutor your child all change, even though the school may fly the same curriculum flag. Check the new emirate's authority rather than assuming Dubai's rules travel. IB Gram explains these bodies and links to them; it is not approved, accredited or licensed by any of them, and no tutoring provider should claim otherwise.

sections.heading: Ministry of Education equivalency, and the mistake made in Year 10
paragraphs: Equivalency is the process by which a secondary certificate earned on an international curriculum is recognised for UAE purposes, including university admission. For Jumeirah 1 families with a UAE university in view, it is a planning constraint that has to be understood in Year 10, because the subjects a student takes and the grades they achieve are what the process looks at.

On the British track, the published requirements are specific. A student must submit proof of one accredited subject at the Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at the Advanced Subsidiary Level with the same grade, and must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3. Arabic and Islamic Education are not included among those five required subjects, which is the detail families most often get wrong.

On the American track, English proficiency requires a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL internet-based test, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, and mathematics requires at least 450 in the SAT Math test before applying. One ranking competitor publishes a six-subject IGCSE requirement, which does not match the sourced guidance. Publishing the correct rule is not a small thing when the wrong one is circulating.

Two cautions. No IB points threshold for equivalency appears in the sourced guidance, so this page does not publish one; ask the Ministry or the attestation authority directly rather than trusting a figure in an advertisement. And equivalency is a regulatory process carried out by the authority, not by a tutoring provider. IB Gram describes it and points you to the official channel. No tutoring is required for it, and anyone implying otherwise is making a false-urgency claim about a government process.

sections.heading: A fuller week: scheduling tuition around a two-curriculum timetable
paragraphs: Students in Dubai private schools carry the mandatory subjects on top of their international curriculum, and the practical effect is fewer free periods and a fuller week than the same programme would occupy elsewhere. For a Year 11 or Diploma student in Jumeirah 1, that means tuition has to be scheduled with more care, and the temptation to add three or four weekly sessions is more damaging here than in a lighter week.

The rule that holds is narrowness. One or two subjects, chosen because that is demonstrably where marks are being lost, with homework set and checked between sessions. Tutoring in four subjects at one session each reliably produces no change in any of them, because the student has no time to do the independent work that converts understanding into retention. In a fuller timetable this effect is sharper, not milder.

The mandatory subjects themselves respond well to a different shape of support. Because the content is prescribed and specific, and because the use of different or additional content without Ministry permission is prohibited, the useful work is structured recall of the set material rather than broad enrichment. Shorter and more frequent beats longer and occasional, which also mirrors how the subjects are timetabled on a forty-minute lesson unit.

Ramadan deserves explicit planning in this district. School hours shorten, afternoons are low-energy for fasting students, and a 16:00 session is usually the least productive hour available. Moving to a post-Iftar slot for the month produces better work in less time. Because tutors are matched across time zones rather than from one city, holding a later evening slot for several weeks is straightforward.

sections.heading: What the Jumeirah 1 school run actually costs in time
paragraphs: By Dubai standards this district is well served. Emirates International School Jumeirah sits on the beach road, Al Ittihad Private School Jumeira and JSS Private School are within the district, Latifa School for Girls has been here for decades, and the Al Safa cluster of Jumeirah College, Jumeirah Primary School, Jumeira Baccalaureate School and Horizon English School is a short drive south. Dubai Japanese School is in Al Wasl.

The constraint is not distance, it is the two roads. Jumeirah Beach Road and Al Wasl Road both carry the district's entire school traffic within the same twenty minutes each morning, and they do not widen. A journey that takes nine minutes at 11:00 takes twenty-five at 07:30. In the afternoon the same compression happens in reverse, which is why a realistic first tuition slot in this district starts around 16:30 for primary children and 17:00 for secondary.

One further local factor matters for scheduling. Because schools are close, a higher share of Jumeirah 1 children are collected by a parent rather than bussed, and many go to after-school activity in the same corridor. That means the gap between school ending and a usable study hour is filled with driving, and the evening is shorter than the short commute suggests.

Where a household has several children at the same nearby school, the pattern that works is consecutive online slots on the same evening: the youngest first for a shorter session while concentration lasts, the older child later. Nothing has to be driven anywhere between the two, which recovers the time the beach road takes in the morning.

sections.heading: The home-tutor search, and what changes when Arabic moves online
paragraphs: Parents here search for home tutors because it is the established phrase in this market, and the honest answer is useful. In-home tutoring in Dubai is widely sold, with market rates running roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour including travel, against roughly AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor online. The premium buys physical presence, which has real value for younger children and for building a working habit.

IB Gram does not provide home visits in the UAE. That is a service we offer only in India, and every country page on this site says the same. What we provide to Jumeirah 1 households is one-to-one tuition over live video. For the mandatory subjects this matters more than it might seem: the pool of tutors qualified to teach Arabic as a first language at secondary level, in Standard Arabic, to a school's prescribed units is not large, and narrowing it to people who can drive to this district at a particular hour makes it considerably smaller.

Arabic teaching online has one genuine requirement worth stating: the student needs to write. Reading and listening transfer to a screen without difficulty, but Standard Arabic written accuracy is built by writing, which means either a graphics tablet or a workflow where the student writes on paper, photographs it and the tutor annotates. Sessions that are all discussion and no writing do not move a first-language grade.

For Islamic Education and Social Studies, where the assessment rewards accurate recall of prescribed content, online delivery is a good fit because the work is structured questioning and correction. The tutor supports the material the school is required to teach rather than importing alternative content, which is both a regulatory point and a practical one: the student is assessed on the set syllabus.

sections.heading: Getting started from Jumeirah 1, and what we will not claim
paragraphs: Start with four facts: the examination board and syllabus code for each international subject, which Arabic stream your child sits and at what level, the school's assessment calendar for the mandatory subjects, and the hours your household can genuinely hold. With those, matching takes one conversation. Without them, the first sessions are spent working out what the problem is, which you are paying for.

Then a trial session with the named tutor who would take the slot. For Arabic in particular, ask for a trial that includes written work rather than conversation, because conversation flatters a dialect speaker and tells you nothing about the register the course assesses. If the fit is wrong we rematch rather than persuade you to continue.

Three things we will not claim. We are not approved, accredited or licensed by KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and no tutoring provider in this market holds a regulator's endorsement of its teaching. We do not perform or guarantee equivalency or attestation; we describe the process and point you to the authority. And we do not offer a grade, a point total or a promised jump in marks, because nobody can honestly sell one.

One piece of regulatory homework applies to any tutor you engage, including independently. Private tutoring in the UAE requires a MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years, with eligible categories including registered school teachers, government and private sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. MoHRE's own service page is the official application route, and those tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws.

process.title: Establish both halves of the timetable
process.description: The first conversation covers the international subjects with their boards and syllabus codes, and the mandatory subjects with the stream and level your child sits. Families are often clear about the first and vague about the second, which is why Arabic grades surprise people.

process.title: Assess the written language, not the spoken
process.description: For Arabic first-language students the diagnostic is a piece of written work in Standard Arabic. Spoken fluency in a dialect tells you almost nothing about the register the course assesses, and assessing the wrong thing is how families spend a year on practice that does not move the grade.

process.title: Trial with the stream specialist
process.description: One session with the person who would teach, in the correct stream. Arabic as a first language and Arabic as an additional language are taught by different specialists, in line with how schools are required to organise the classes, and a tutor strong in one is not automatically strong in the other.

process.title: Fit the sessions to a fuller week
process.description: Dubai students carry the mandatory subjects on top of their international curriculum, so the week has fewer gaps. We schedule one or two subjects properly rather than four superficially, place mandatory-subject work in shorter frequent slots, and move to post-Iftar timing during Ramadan.

process.title: Review against a named target
process.description: Every booking has something specific attached: a component, an assessment point, a piece of written work. We review on a fixed date rather than continuing by default, and when the student can do the thing unaided we say so and step the booking down or close it.

whyPoints.title: The mandatory subjects are treated as subjects
whyPoints.description: Arabic, Islamic Education and UAE Social Studies are mandatory in every Dubai private school, and this page treats them as real courses with real standards rather than as a footnote. No competitor page in this market addresses them beyond a subject chip.

whyPoints.title: Arabic streams kept separate
whyPoints.description: First-language and additional-language Arabic are different courses with different expectations, and KHDA requires schools to teach them in separate classes. We match a specialist to the stream rather than offering one Arabic tutor for both, because the written-register work that a first-language student needs is specific.

whyPoints.title: Regulators explained, never claimed
whyPoints.description: KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, the Ras Al Khaimah Department of Knowledge and the Ministry of Education each govern different emirates, and their powers differ. We explain what each does and link to it. We are not approved, accredited or licensed by any of them.

whyPoints.title: The sourced equivalency rule, not the circulating one
whyPoints.description: The British track requires five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic Education excluded, plus one A Level or two AS Levels at E. A ranking competitor publishes six subjects. We publish the sourced figure and point you to the authority to verify.

whyPoints.title: Scheduling built for a fuller timetable
whyPoints.description: Students here carry two curricula, so the week has fewer gaps than the programme suggests. One or two subjects supported properly beats four supported superficially, and mandatory-subject work suits shorter, more frequent sessions that mirror how it is timetabled.

whyPoints.title: Writing built into Arabic sessions
whyPoints.description: Online Arabic that is all discussion does not move a first-language grade, because written accuracy in Standard Arabic is built by writing. Sessions use a graphics tablet or a photograph-and-annotate workflow so the student produces written work every week.

faqs.question: Does my child have to study Arabic if they are in a British or IB school in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Yes. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and the federal position is that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies while adhering to the Ministry's general regulations. Which Arabic stream a child sits depends on whether they are classified as an Arab or non-Arab student, and KHDA requires those classes to be organised separately because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ.

faqs.question: My child speaks Arabic at home but gets mediocre Arabic grades. Why?
faqs.answer: Almost always because the course assesses Standard Arabic and the fluency is in a spoken dialect. Arabic as a first language is taught and examined in Standard Arabic against first-language expectations: formal grammar, classical and modern literary texts and sustained academic writing. A child who converses easily can still be weak on written register and formal accuracy, and those are the things being marked. It is a teachable gap and it responds quickly, provided the teaching targets written formal Arabic rather than general conversation practice.

faqs.question: What is the difference between the two Arabic streams a Dubai school runs?
faqs.answer: They are different courses. Arabic as a first language carries first-language expectations in Standard Arabic, covering grammar, literature and extended writing. Arabic as an additional language is an acquisition course building reading, listening, speaking and writing to a defined level. KHDA requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, and states that combined classes for both groups are prohibited because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. A tutor strong in one stream is not automatically suited to the other.

faqs.question: How much Arabic and Islamic Education time does a Dubai school have to provide?
faqs.answer: KHDA calculates mandatory-subject instructional time on a forty-minute lesson unit. Schools may vary the length of individual lessons provided the total weekly time is met, and KHDA advises that the length of any mandatory-subject lesson should be at least twenty-five minutes. Schools are also required to ensure that teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects. For the mandatory UAE subjects, using different or additional content without prior Ministry permission is prohibited, which constrains what any tutor can legitimately introduce.

faqs.question: How many IGCSE subjects does a UAE student need for equivalency?
faqs.answer: On the British track the sourced requirement is five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, alongside one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic Education are not included among those five required subjects. One ranking competitor states six subjects, which does not match the sourced guidance. Requirements can change, so verify the current rule with the Ministry of Education or your emirate's attestation authority before planning around it.

faqs.question: What does the IB Diploma need for UAE equivalency?
faqs.answer: This page does not publish an IB points threshold, and you should be cautious about any provider that does. The sourced equivalency guidance covers the British and American tracks in detail and states no IB points figure, so any number circulating in tutoring advertisements is unverified. Ask the Ministry of Education or your emirate's attestation authority directly, because they operate the process and publish the current requirement. Equivalency is also a regulatory process the authority performs, not something a tutoring provider can carry out, expedite or guarantee on your behalf.

faqs.question: Which schools are actually inside Jumeirah 1?
faqs.answer: Emirates International School Jumeirah runs the IB continuum on the beach road, and Al Ittihad Private School Jumeira, JSS Private School and Latifa School for Girls all sit within the district. Dubai Japanese School is in neighbouring Al Wasl. For secondary, most Jumeirah 1 families also look at the Al Safa cluster a short drive south: Jumeirah College, Jumeirah Primary School, Jumeira Baccalaureate School and Horizon English School, with Kings' School Dubai and Raffles World Academy further along towards Umm Suqeim. All of them deliver the mandatory UAE subjects alongside their licensed curriculum.

faqs.question: Can a tutor come to our villa in Jumeirah 1?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram delivers all UAE tutoring online, one-to-one, over live video, and does not send tutors to addresses anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. For the mandatory subjects this is a genuine advantage rather than a compromise. The pool of tutors qualified to teach Arabic as a first language at secondary level in Standard Arabic is not large, and requiring them to drive to this district at a fixed hour would shrink your choice considerably.

faqs.question: Does online teaching work for Arabic writing?
faqs.answer: It does, provided the session includes writing. Reading and listening transfer to a screen easily, but written accuracy in Standard Arabic is built by writing, so a session that is all discussion will not move a first-language grade. Two workflows solve this: a graphics tablet, which lets tutor and student write on the same page in real time, or a routine where the student writes on paper, photographs it and the tutor annotates it live. Ask for a trial session that includes written work rather than only conversation.

faqs.question: We may move to Abu Dhabi. Do the same education rules apply?
faqs.answer: Not entirely, and this trips families up. In Dubai, KHDA oversees private education quality. In Abu Dhabi and Al Ain, ADEK supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools, and its professional-ethics rules bar private and charter school staff from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school. Sharjah's authority and Ras Al Khaimah's Department of Knowledge also approve tuition fees, curricula, programmes and assessment methods. The Ministry of Education supervises Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. Check the new emirate's authority rather than assuming Dubai's framework travels.

faqs.question: How many subjects should we tutor at once if the week is already full?
faqs.answer: One or two, and fewer than you think. Students in Dubai private schools carry the mandatory UAE subjects on top of their international curriculum, so the week genuinely has fewer gaps than the programme suggests. A weekly hour spread across four subjects reliably changes none of them, because the student has no time left for the independent practice that turns understanding into retention. Pick the one or two subjects where marks are demonstrably being lost, identified from mock scripts and mark schemes rather than from an impression.

faqs.question: Should Jumeirah 1 lessons shift to a post-Iftar slot through Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Yes, and in this district we would suggest it as the default. School hours shorten during Ramadan, afternoons are low-energy for fasting students, and a 16:00 session tends to be the least productive hour of the day. A post-Iftar slot generally produces better work in less time. Because tutors are matched across time zones rather than drawn from one city, holding a later evening slot for several weeks is straightforward. The same flexibility applies around Eid and over the long summer break, where a short intensive block often beats a weekly rhythm.

faqs.question: Is Arabic as a Group 1 Diploma subject a good idea for a bilingual student?
faqs.answer: It can be an asset, and the decision should be made on written evidence rather than on how a student speaks. Taking Arabic as a Group 1 language and literature subject means literary analysis at Higher or Standard Level in Standard Arabic, which is a serious commitment; Group 2 is a different proposition. The useful step is an honest assessment of written Standard Arabic in MYP 4 or Year 10, because that is when the decision can still be shaped. Discovering the gap in the first term of Diploma Year 1 is a much harder position.

faqs.question: What time can lessons start given the beach road traffic?
faqs.answer: For primary children collected by a parent, 16:30 is usually achievable. For secondary students, plan for 17:00 or later. The constraint in Jumeirah 1 is not distance but the two roads: Jumeirah Beach Road and Al Wasl Road carry the whole district's school traffic inside the same twenty minutes, and a nine-minute off-peak journey can take twenty-five at school-run time. Because a higher share of children here are collected rather than bussed, the gap between school ending and a usable study hour is often filled with driving and an activity.

faqs.question: Does a tutor need a licence to teach privately in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by permit. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers categories including teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. MoHRE's own service page, Issuance of a New Work Permit for Private Tutor Licensing, is the official application route. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, with no published schedule of amounts.

dubai/jumeirah-1.closingHeading: Both halves of the week, or neither works
dubai/jumeirah-1.closingBody: A Jumeirah 1 student is carrying an international curriculum and a set of mandatory UAE subjects at the same time, and a tutoring plan that ignores half of that will not hold. Settle which Arabic stream your child sits and at what level, get the board and syllabus code for the international subjects, and ask the school for both assessment calendars. From there, matching is one conversation and a trial session with the named tutor, including written work where Arabic is involved. All lessons run online, one-to-one, over live video.

dubai/jumeirah-2.tutorsIntro: The tutors here are chosen partly for availability. A specialist who can only teach at 15:00 is of no use to a Jumeirah 2 family, so matching takes the household's actual window first and then finds the subject specialist who fits inside it.

intro.heading: The school run decides everything else in Jumeirah 2
paragraphs: Jumeirah 2 is a villa district between Jumeirah Beach Road and Al Wasl Road, with Town Centre Jumeirah and Sunset Mall at its spine and Jumeirah Beach Park at its southern edge. It is a settled, family-heavy neighbourhood where most children are collected by a parent or a driver rather than bussed, because the schools are close enough that a bus makes little sense. That single detail reshapes the afternoon more than anything about the curriculum.

A bussed child comes home once, at a predictable time, and the afternoon is then free. A collected child generates two journeys in the afternoon rather than one, and the parent doing the collecting is also the person who would otherwise be supervising homework. Add an activity in the same corridor, which is almost universal here, and the afternoon fills with driving. Families consistently describe having no time, and they are right: the time exists but it is distributed into fragments too short to use.

The second constraint is the roads. Jumeirah Beach Road and Al Wasl Road carry this district's entire school traffic inside the same twenty-minute window, twice a day, and neither widens. A journey that takes nine minutes at 11:00 takes twenty-five at 07:30 and again at 14:30. There is no clever route. The implication for tutoring is specific: the earliest hour a secondary student in Jumeirah 2 can reliably start work is around 17:00, and anything booked before that will be cancelled often enough to break the habit.

The third is sport. This district runs on swimming, tennis, football and beach activity, much of it between 16:00 and 18:30, because that is when the facilities are usable for much of the year. Families who try to schedule tutoring against the activity schedule rather than around it lose, every time. The sensible approach is to accept that two or three weekday evenings are committed and place the tutoring on the ones that are not.

What makes this worth a page of its own is that scheduling, not teaching quality, is the commonest reason tutoring fails to produce anything. A tutor who is excellent but booked at an impossible hour will be cancelled twice a month, the sessions will fall out of sequence, homework will not be done between them, and after a term the family will conclude that tutoring does not work. The tutoring was never the variable.

Everything on this page is delivered as one-to-one tuition over live video. IB Gram does not send tutors to addresses in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. The scheduling advantage of that is not marginal in a district like this: no travel time on either side means a 19:30 slot is as easy to hold as a 17:00 one, a session can be moved by a day without anyone losing a journey, and two children can be placed back to back on the same evening.

dubai/jumeirah-2.programmesIntro: Each programme makes different demands on the week, and knowing which demand falls where is how a realistic schedule gets built. These are the four that matter for Jumeirah 2 households.

programmes.name: Key Stage 1-2 and the Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Short attention spans and early bedtimes make this the stage where timing matters most. A forty-five minute session at 16:30 produces more than ninety minutes at 19:00, because a nine-year-old at 19:00 has nothing left. The work itself is usually number fluency, reading or written methods rather than anything conceptual.
programmes.countryNote: Jumeirah 2 primary children are collected rather than bussed and usually go straight to an activity, so the realistic primary slot is either immediately after school at 16:00 to 16:30, or on a weekend morning. Weekend mornings work better here than in most districts because activity schedules are weekday-heavy.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Four criteria per subject, each marked out of eight. MYP students have enough homework to fill an evening and not yet the self-management to protect a study hour, which is why a fixed external appointment helps them more than it helps either younger or older students.
programmes.countryNote: MYP 5 carries the Personal Project, and in a district where evenings are committed to sport this is the piece that quietly slips. Blocking the project into weekend mornings across a term, rather than hoping weekday evenings open up, is what works for Jumeirah 2 families.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: Nine or ten subjects examined at the end of Year 11, which turns Year 11 into a scheduling problem as much as an academic one. Students need to run a revision programme across all of them, and the arithmetic of a Jumeirah 2 week decides how much of that is actually possible.
programmes.countryNote: Cambridge allocates every examination centre to one of six administrative timetable zones and states that the correct version of the timetable for the zone must be used. Ask your exams officer for the centre's own timetable early, because revision planning backwards from the wrong dates is worse than not planning at all.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Diploma students work later and better in the evening than younger students, so a 20:00 slot is genuinely productive here. Their problem is not the hour but the collision of coursework deadlines with mock examinations.
programmes.countryNote: UAE schools sit the May session, so for a Jumeirah 2 Diploma student the committed period runs from November through February, when internal coursework deadlines and mocks overlap. Confirm every IB date with your child's Diploma coordinator, since the IB is the only authoritative source for its own calendar.

dubai/jumeirah-2.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects Jumeirah 2 families book most, with a note on how much weekly time each realistically needs. Time demand matters as much as difficulty when the week is already full.

subjects.name: IGCSE Mathematics
subjects.description: Benefits more than any other subject from two shorter sessions a week rather than one long one, because fluency is built by spaced practice. The tier decision between Extended or Higher and Core or Foundation sets the ceiling and should be settled before booking.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Needs independent problem practice between sessions, so a weekly slot without homework time around it achieves little. Higher Level Paper 3 is an extended investigation that requires its own block of practice rather than general revision.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics with a heavy emphasis on interpreting results in context. Technology use means sessions work well on a shared screen, and the exploration suits data a student can collect in a few committed sittings.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL · IGCSE 0625 and 4PH1
subjects.description: Explanation questions wanting a mechanism rather than a formula are the reliable loss point. Sessions are most productive when the student brings a marked script, because physics errors are specific and visible on paper.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL · IGCSE 0620 and 4CH1
subjects.description: Mole calculations and organic chemistry carry the grade. The Diploma investigation needs a sustained block of time for data collection, which in this district means planning it into a holiday rather than an evening.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL · IGCSE 0610 and 4BI1
subjects.description: Content-heavy and therefore well suited to short frequent sessions with retrieval practice between them. Command terms decide marks more than content volume does, and correcting command-term habits is quick work.

subjects.name: English Language and Literature
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL · IGCSE First Language English
subjects.description: Writing subjects need the student to write between sessions, which is the hardest thing to protect in a committed week. One longer weekend session often works better than a short weekday one for drafting and redrafting.

subjects.name: Economics and Business Management
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL · IGCSE Business Studies
subjects.description: Essay and case-study technique responds quickly to correction, so a short block of four to six sessions before a mock often does more than a year of weekly support.

subjects.name: MYP subjects across all criteria
subjects.description: Criterion-led marking means the gap is usually in communication and reflection rather than knowledge. A fixed weekly appointment helps MYP students specifically, because they have the workload without the self-management yet.

subjects.name: Arabic and the mandatory UAE subjects
subjects.description: Mandatory in every Dubai private school whatever the licensed curriculum, with separate classes required for Arabs and non-Arabs. These suit short frequent sessions, mirroring how they are timetabled on a forty-minute lesson unit.

sections.heading: What a Jumeirah 2 weekday actually looks like
paragraphs: Published advice on tutoring assumes a weekday with empty afternoons in it. That is not the weekday this district has. Working through it hour by hour is more useful than any general recommendation about how often a child should be tutored, because it shows exactly which hours exist and which do not.

The morning is lost to the run. Jumeirah Beach Road and Al Wasl Road absorb the district's school traffic inside the same twenty minutes, and a nine-minute off-peak journey becomes twenty-five. Afternoon pickup compresses the same way in reverse from around 14:15. For a parent doing both ends of that, the window between arriving home and starting the evening is genuinely short.

The afternoon then divides into fragments. School ends, a child is collected, an activity starts somewhere between 16:00 and 16:30, the activity ends between 17:30 and 18:30, and dinner follows. None of those gaps is long enough to do useful academic work in, and the gap that is long enough arrives at around 19:00 for a secondary student, by which point a primary child is heading for bed.

The table below sets out the hours and what each is good for. The most useful column is the last one, which lists what should not be booked at that hour. Most failed tutoring arrangements in districts like this were booked into an hour from that column, and the failure was predictable from the calendar before the first session.

sections.heading: Session length and frequency by year group
paragraphs: Tutoring in this market is usually sold in hours because an hour is a convenient billing unit, not because an hour is the right length for every student. For a seven-year-old it is roughly twice too long; for a Diploma student working through a past paper it is sometimes too short. Matching length to year group is a free improvement that most families never make.

The governing variable is sustained attention, and it rises steeply with age. A primary child can concentrate properly for twenty to thirty minutes, which means a forty-five minute session with a break is productive and a sixty-minute one has fifteen minutes of theatre at the end. By MYP 4 a full hour works. By Diploma, ninety minutes is often better than sixty, because setting up a problem and seeing it through takes time.

Frequency matters more than length for anything requiring fluency. Mathematics in particular responds to spacing: two thirty or forty-five minute sessions a week build retention that one ninety-minute session does not, because the forgetting happens between sessions and the second session interrupts it. For content-heavy subjects taught in blocks, one longer session plus structured retrieval practice in between is usually enough.

The table gives a starting point. Treat the final column as the reasoning rather than the rule, because a particular child may differ. What should not differ is the principle: fewer subjects supported properly beats more subjects supported superficially, especially in a week with as little slack as this district's.

sections.heading: The UAE academic year, and where revision actually fits
paragraphs: A term-time week has little slack in this district, so a serious plan uses the shape of the year rather than fighting it. The UAE academic calendar has its own rhythm, and Ramadan moves earlier each year, which means the relationship between Ramadan and the examination season shifts and has to be checked rather than assumed.

Autumn is the cheapest time to buy support and the time families are least inclined to. Nothing is urgent in October, which is exactly why a diagnosed gap closes quickly then. By February the same gap costs more effort because it is competing with coursework deadlines, mocks and revision. The single highest-return decision most families could make is to move their tutoring six months earlier.

Ramadan deserves its own plan rather than a pause. School hours shorten, afternoons are low-energy for fasting students and the usual 17:00 slot becomes the worst hour of the day. A post-Iftar session typically produces better work in less time, and because tutors are matched across time zones a later slot is straightforward to hold for the month. Families who simply stop for Ramadan lose four weeks at the point in the year when they can least afford to.

The table sets out the year and what each period suits. The pattern worth noticing is that the periods when families most want to book are the periods when support does the least, and the periods when nobody is thinking about tutoring are when it is most effective.
